Learning-Augmented Online Scheduling
with Parsimonious Preemption

Mugen Blue ††thanks: University of California, Santa Cruz, US. (msblue@ucsc.edu, sim9@ucsc.edu). Supported in part by NSF awards CCF-2535599, 2537126, and 2423106, and by ONR grant N00014-22-1-2701.    Sungjin Im11footnotemark: 1    Alexander Lindermayr ††thanks: Institut für Mathematik, Technische Universität Berlin, Germany. alexander.lindermayr@tu-berlin.de.
Abstract

Learning-augmented algorithms have emerged as a powerful paradigm to surpass traditional worst-case lower bounds by integrating potentially noisy predictions. While this framework has seen success in online scheduling, existing work primarily optimizes job latency while relying on frequent, “blind” preemptions. This ignores the fundamental trade-off between algorithmic performance and preemption complexity. We provide the first systematic study of learning-augmented scheduling that curbs preemption while optimizing latency. We establish that the gap between theoretical latency bounds and preemption overhead can be bridged with solid analytical foundations. Our results include O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive algorithms for single and unrelated parallel machines with only O⁡(1)O(1) preemptions per job under accurate predictions, with overhead scaling logarithmically with the prediction error. By providing the first bounded-preemption guarantees for unrelated and malleable machines, we extend the theoretical reach of the learning-augmented framework to more constrained and realistic settings. Finally, our algorithms are validated through experiments.

1 Introduction

The paradigm of learning-augmented algorithms has recently emerged as a powerful framework for overcoming the limitations of worst-case analysis [MV22]. By incorporating potentially noisy machine-learning predictions into algorithm design, this framework enables algorithms that are both consistent—near-optimal when predictions are accurate—and robust—with worst-case guarantees even under adversarial predictions. This approach is especially effective for online algorithms, where predictions can mitigate future uncertainty that is unavoidable in traditional worst-case models.

Online scheduling is a prominent application of this paradigm. Traditionally, algorithms often suffer from limited information about key parameters; a central example is the non-clairvoyance, where job sizes are unknown until completion [MPT94, Edm00]. A growing literature shows that online algorithms can substantially benefit from job-size predictions when minimizing latency [PSK18, Mit20, Im+23, ALT21, ZLZ22].

However, in practical systems such as large-scale data centers, preemption and migration can incur substantial overheads, including context-switching costs and cache invalidation [MB91, Tsa07, Ver+15]. Although preemption-aware scheduling is well studied in systems research, from mechanisms such as preemption thresholds [SW00] and deferred-preemption heuristics [DB12] to production-scale data-center resource management [Ver+15, CRZ17], these approaches are largely qualitative and offer few provable guarantees on job latency, particularly under prediction error.

We argue that the absence of an analytical framework for this trade-off remains a significant gap in the learning-augmented literature. We address this gap by using predictions to design the first algorithms that minimize total completion time while using preemption parsimoniously. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study to analytically ground the trade-off between job latency and preemption complexity under job-size predictions. Our results move beyond the “blind” preemption required by classical non-clairvoyant models and provide the first bounded-preemption guarantees for unrelated and malleable machine settings.

1.1 Summary of our results

Problem setup: We assume all nn jobs are available at time t=0t=0, because i) simultaneous arrival serves as a fundamental baseline in scheduling theory; and ii) while extensions to arbitrary arrival times are possible, they can obscure the core analytical ideas. We therefore provide a sketch of the extensions in the appendix to maintain a transparent presentation of our main results.

For each job jj, we know its predicted requirement p^j\hat{p}_{j}. In practice, these predictions p^j\hat{p}_{j} are typically derived by profiling the resource consumption of recurring jobs or by applying statistical models to historical execution traces from the cluster [Fai+24, Par+18]. A job jj completes once it has been processed by its requirement pjp_{j}. However, the exact processing requirements remain unknown until completion; this setting is referred to as non-clairvoyant scheduling (when predictions are unavailable), in contrast to clairvoyant scheduling, where job sizes are known (upon arrival).

We focus on minimizing the total completion time objective, ∑jCj\sum_{j}C_{j}, where CjC_{j} is the completion time of job jj. Since we evaluate the online algorithm relative to an optimum multiplicatively, our goal is equivalently stated as minimizing the average completion time. An algorithm is cc-competitive if its total completion time is at most cc times that of the offline optimum for all inputs.

We first present our findings under the assumption that all predictions are underestimates (i.e., p^j≤pj\hat{p}_{j}\leq p_{j} for all jobs jj). Subsequently, we introduce a robust framework to handle overestimated job requirements. We define D⁡(p,p^):=∑j(log2⁡(pj/p^j)+1)D(p,\hat{p}):=\sum_{j}(\log_{2}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})+1) as the ideal benchmark for the number of preemptions; we denote this simply as DD when the context is clear. This benchmark is motivated by the fact that any non-clairvoyant algorithm performing o⁡(log⁡pj)o(\log p_{j}) preemptions, even for a single job jj, necessarily has a competitive ratio of Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) (see Theorem A.1 in the appendix). Consequently, if p^j=1\hat{p}_{j}=1 for all jj, any algorithm must perform Ω⁡(D)\Omega(D) preemptions to remain competitive.

Our results are summarized below. This is the first work to demonstrate how predictions can be utilized to minimize preemption. We provide constant-competitive algorithms while bounding the number of preemptions per job to within a constant factor of the benchmark DD.

  • •

    Single machine: In the single-machine setting, which serves as a warm-up for our study, only one job can be processed at a time. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, we provide an algorithm that is (2+ε)(2+\varepsilon)-competitive while incurring at most O⁡(1ε​D)O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}D) preemptions (Theorem 2.1). This guarantee extends to identical parallel machines (Theorem C.1).

  • •

    Unrelated machines: This is our main result. In this heterogeneous parallel machine environment, each job jj is processed at a rate of λi​j\lambda_{ij} on machine i∈Mi\in M. A machine can process at most one job at a time. For this problem, we give a 14.48​(1+ε)14.48(1+\varepsilon)-competitive algorithm that performs at most O⁡(1ε3​D)O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}D) preemptions (Theorems 3.3 and 3.4).

  • •

    Malleable job scheduling: In this setting, jobs can be assigned to multiple machines (processors) simultaneously to expedite processing subject to eligibility constraints. Each job jj is associated with a concave speed-up function that determines the processing rate based on the number of machines assigned. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, we provide an algorithm that is 27​ee−1​(1+ε)27\frac{e}{e-1}(1+\varepsilon)-competitive, making at most O⁡(1ε3​D)O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}D) preemptions (Theorem 4.5); see Theorem F.1 for a slightly better bound on identical parallel machines.

We remark that our results extend readily to weighted jobs by considering the weighted objective ∑jwj​Cj\sum_{j}w_{j}C_{j} and the weighted preemption benchmark D⁡(p,p^):=∑jwj​(log2⁡(pj/p^j)+1)D(p,\hat{p}):=\sum_{j}w_{j}(\log_{2}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})+1). For clarity of presentation, we focus on the unweighted case throughout the paper.

We also validate our algorithms through experiments, including heuristic adaptations of the theoretical versions developed in this paper. The results demonstrate that our algorithms effectively optimize total completion time while utilizing preemptions parsimoniously

Handling overestimation.

Interestingly, overestimates are not symmetric to underestimates. To minimize total completion time, one must intuitively complete many jobs as quickly as possible [Smi56]. Without knowledge about which jobs are short, we must hedge against short jobs being delayed by long ones via exponentially increasing our guesses; if a job does not complete after (1+δ)k(1+\delta)^{k} units of processing, we switch to other jobs, assuming its requirement is at least (1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k+1}, for some constant δ>0\delta>0. Underestimations allow us to skip many initial guesses, but overestimations are less helpful: if all jobs are overestimated to the same requirement, the predictions provide no useful prioritization.

In fact, if we treat overestimated jobs identically to underestimated ones, the competitive ratio can degrade to O⁡(maxj⁡p^j/pj)O(\max_{j}\hat{p}_{j}/p_{j}). A more robust approach is to intentionally underestimate job requirements by scaling down the initially provided estimates. This ensures that only a small number of jobs, gg, remain overpredicted. We execute the algorithm for underestimated jobs until the number of unfinished jobs drops to g/εg/\varepsilon. At this transition point, we reset the predictions for all remaining jobs to ensure they are henceforth treated as underestimates. This strategy maintains the competitive ratio while incurring only O⁡(gε2​log2​pmax)O(\frac{g}{\varepsilon^{2}}\log_{2}p_{\max}) additional preemptions; see Theorem 2.2 for details.

As long as gg is sublinear in nn and job requirements are polynomial in nn, a common and realistic scenario, the impact of overestimated jobs on the total number of preemptions is asymptotically negligible. Furthermore, a single global parameter gg, which represents an upper bound on the number of overestimations, is arguably easier to predict accurately than jobs’ individual sizes. This strategy successfully extends to the other settings considered in this work (Section D).

1.2 Our approaches and contributions

To understand the challenge of minimizing preemptions, note that we cannot use the popular Round-Robin (RR) algorithm. RR cycles through active jobs and processes each for one unit, resulting in prohibitively many preemptions. Despite this drawback, RR has been widely used in the learning-augmented literature because it is memoryless: its execution depends only on the set of currently active jobs [PSK18, LM25, Im+23]. Thus, if each instantaneous schedule approximates RR, we obtain a comparable performance guarantee; this is the basis of our approach.

To avoid excessive preemptions, we consider a less preemptive algorithm called Multi-Level Feedback (MLF) [MPT94]. MLF maintains multiple FIFO queues to process jobs; for some constant δ>0\delta>0, the kk-th queue contains jobs that have been processed for at least (1+δ)k(1+\delta)^{k} and less than (1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k+1} units of time. A non-clairvoyant algorithm, given no predictions, initially places each job in the queue corresponding to the smallest k≥0k\geq 0.

In our variant, which we call Predicted Multi-Level Feedback (PMLF), a new job starts in the queue corresponding to its predicted requirement p^j\hat{p}_{j}, rather than in the first queue. If all predictions are underestimates (p^j≤pj\hat{p}_{j}\leq p_{j}), we show that PMLF achieves an O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive ratio while incurring O⁡(D)=O⁡(∑j(1+log1+δ⁡(pj/p^j)))O(D)=O(\sum_{j}(1+\log_{1+\delta}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j}))) preemptions. Hence, when predictions are accurate, we perform only O⁡(1)O(1) preemptions per job on average.

Our main result is the Simulated Non-preemptive Adaptive Prediction (SNAP) algorithm for unrelated machines. SNAP is designed to handle the complexities of unrelated machines, the most general parallel-machine model in classical scheduling theory [LST90, Sku01, Hal+97]. Here, we cannot simply use a processing queue based on elapsed work, because the processing speeds λi​j\lambda_{ij} are unique to each job-machine pair: a given machine may be highly efficient for one job and extremely slow for another.

A prominent non-clairvoyant algorithm for unrelated machines is Proportional Fairness (PF), which identifies job processing rates that maximize their product, a task reducible to a convex program. This is not a computational bottleneck; rather, it enables efficient schedule computation, since the objective can be approximated to arbitrary precision in near-linear time [CMP22]. However, a PF schedule is highly fractional (it alternates between multiple feasible schedules11 1 A feasible schedule at each time can be thought of as a matching between jobs and machines.) and is therefore highly preemptive. Furthermore, PF must recompute the rates whenever a job arrives or completes.

To address this, SNAP operates through a sequence of disjoint epochs. At the start of each epoch, the algorithm runs PF to compute the desired job processing rates. It then uses predicted job requirements to define the next checkpoint for each job: the smallest power of 1+δ1+\delta that is greater than both p^j\hat{p}_{j} and the current amount of processing the job has received. This strategy limits the total number of preemptions to a logarithmic factor of the multiplicative estimation error. We then choose an epoch duration so that, under PF, a β\beta-fraction of jobs reach their next checkpoints. The preemptions made in the epoch are charged to the jobs that reached their checkpoints, and our algorithm remains O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive because we follow PF for a 1−β1-\beta fraction of jobs. Finally, we convert this virtual preemptive schedule into a non-preemptive schedule using an offline rounding procedure and run it.

For malleable jobs, however, we use a different approach. The reason is that the approximate super-additivity property is not known to hold for this problem, unlike in the unrelated-machines setting (see Lemma 3.10 for details). Therefore, we first analyze a more robust version of the PF algorithm. It is known that PF is O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive for a general class of scheduling problems, called Polytope Scheduling (see Section 4 for the definition) [IKM18, JLM26], which encompasses the malleable-jobs setting. To make PF less preemptive, we consider a version that does not change its rates until a constant fraction of jobs reach their next checkpoint. Here, unlike in SNAP, where we use the known performance guarantee of PF as a black box, we directly modify the analysis of PF from [IKM18, JLM26]. This approach incurs at most O⁡(1ε3​D)O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}D) processing rate changes in total, and by simulating this algorithm as in SNAP with predictions, we obtain the desired result.

1.3 Further related work

We focus on the most closely related work here and defer a broader discussion to Appendix H.

Single and identical machines. In the clairvoyant setting, Shortest Job First (SJF), which processes jobs in non-decreasing order of processing time, is optimal for total completion time [Smi56]. In the non-clairvoyant setting, RR is best-possible 22-competitive [MPT94], but incurs excessively many preemptions. Multilevel (Adaptive) Feedback (MLF) reduces preemptions while remaining O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive, and can be parameterized to be (2+ε)(2+\varepsilon)-competitive for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 [MPT94]. These guarantees for SJF and RR extend to parallel identical machines [MPT94, Bea+12].

Unrelated machines. In the clairvoyant online setting, utilizing immediate-dispatch and non-migratory algorithms while assuming each machine runs SPT, assigning an arriving job to the machine with the least marginal increase in the objective is O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive [AGK12, Gup+20, LM25]. For non-clairvoyant algorithms, SelfishMigrate and Proportional Fairness (PF) were analyzed with competitive ratios of 3232 and 3.623.62, respectively [Im+14, JLM26]. Clairvoyant algorithms were also explored in [Hal+97, Cha+96, LMR23].

Online scheduling with predictions. Various objectives have been considered in the learning-augmented setting, see [LM25a] for an overview. Examples include total completion time [PSK18, Im+23, LM25, Din+22, Las+23], total flow time [ALT21, Mit20], makespan minimization [Lat+20, LX21, Bal+25], and energy consumption [Bam+20, AJS22].

2 Single machine

We start with our first result, which is for scheduling on a single machine. We first present our algorithm Predicted Multi-Level Feedback (PMLF) for a hyperparameter δ>0\delta>0:

  • •

    Maintain a set of FIFO queues {Qi}i≥0\{Q_{i}\}_{i\geq 0}. Initially, place a job jj into QkQ_{k} where ⌊log1+δ⁡p^j⌋\lfloor\log_{1+\delta}\hat{p}_{j}\rfloor.

  • •

    At any time tt, work on the front job of the non-empty queue of the lowest index.

  • •

    If j∈Qij\in Q_{i} was processed by in total by (1+δ)i+1(1+\delta)^{i+1}, move jj from QiQ_{i} to the end of Qi+1Q_{i+1}.

PMLF becomes MLF when p^j=1\hat{p}_{j}=1 for each job jj (under the standard assumption that pj≥1p_{j}\geq 1). For now, we assume that p^j≤pj\hat{p}_{j}\leq p_{j} for each job jj; we will soon discuss how to relax this assumption.

Theorem 2.1.

For any constant δ>0\delta>0, PMLF is (2+2​δ)(2+2\delta)-competitive for minimizing the total completion time on a single machine and performs at most O⁡(1δ​log2⁡(pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\delta}\log_{2}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) preemptions for each job jj if there are only underpredictions.

We sketch the proof of the theorem deferring the full proof to Appendix B. The preemption bound comes from the fact that job jj is preempted only when it is moved between queues, which happens at most ⌊log1+δ⁡pj⌋−⌊log1+δ⁡p^j⌋\lfloor\log_{1+\delta}p_{j}\rfloor-\lfloor\log_{1+\delta}\hat{p}_{j}\rfloor many times. For the competitive ratio, we reuse the standard MLF delay-style analysis of [MPT94]. It is easy to observe that before a job jj completes, any other job ii can be processed for at most min⁡{(1+δ)​pj,pi}\min\{(1+\delta)p_{j},p_{i}\} units of time. If δ\delta is infinitesimally small, the analysis essentially becomes that of Round-Robin, which is known to be 22-competitive [MPT94]. The multiplicative factor 1+δ1+\delta used to define queues inflates the competitive ratio by a factor of 1+δ1+\delta.

Handling overestimations.

If we allow overestimations, let gg be an upper bound on the number of overestimated jobs. By scaling down predicted sizes, we can make gg small at the cost of more preemptions. We consider a variation of PMLF, which uses gg and a parameter γ>0\gamma>0: Let TT be the time when the number of unfinished jobs is at most g/γg/\gamma, and qj​(T)q_{j}(T) denote the cumulative processed size of job jj until time TT. At time TT, move each unfinished job jj to the end of the queue QkQ_{k} where (1+δ)k≤qj​(T)<(1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k}\leq q_{j}(T)<(1+\delta)^{k+1}. Then, we continue with PMLF. We prove in Appendix B:

Theorem 2.2.

If there are at most gg overestimated jobs, then for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, the adapted PMLF is 2​(1+ε)2(1+\varepsilon)-competitive and incurs at most O⁡(1ε​∑j(1+log2⁡pjp^j)+gε2​log2⁡(maxj⁡pj))O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\sum_{j}(1+\log_{2}\frac{p_{j}}{\hat{p}_{j}})+\frac{g}{\varepsilon^{2}}\log_{2}(\max_{j}p_{j})) preemptions.

3 Unrelated machines

In this section, we describe SNAP for scheduling on unrelated machines. We are given a set MM of unrelated machines. Each job jj is available for scheduling from time 0, and we know its predicted size p^j\hat{p}_{j} and processing rates {λi​j}i∈M\{\lambda_{ij}\}_{i\in M} across all machines. We assume that every job jj has processing requirement equal to a power of 1+δ1+\delta for some δ>0\delta>0; that is, pj=(1+δ)ip_{j}=(1+\delta)^{i} for some integer i≥0i\geq 0. If pjp_{j} is not a power of 1+δ1+\delta, we instead treat the job as active until it has been processed for (1+δ)⌈log1+δ⁡pj⌉(1+\delta)^{\lceil\log_{1+\delta}p_{j}\rceil} units of time. This increases the competitive ratio by a factor of at most 1+δ1+\delta. We assume that all job sizes are underestimated, i.e., p^j≤pj\hat{p}_{j}\leq p_{j} for all jobs jj. The case of overestimation is addressed in Appendix D, following the same approach as for the single-machine case.

Before describing SNAP, we introduce checkpoints. We say that a job jj reaches a checkpoint at time tt if its cumulative processed size qj​(t)q_{j}(t) reaches a power of 1+δ1+\delta. For convenience, when a job reaches a checkpoint, we say that it is exhausted (or that an exhaustion occurs). For job jj, we begin tracking checkpoints at its predicted size p^j\hat{p}_{j}: let (1+δ)ρj(1+\delta)^{\rho_{j}} be its first checkpoint, where ρj:=⌈log1+δ⁡p^j⌉\rho_{j}:=\lceil\log_{1+\delta}\hat{p}_{j}\rceil. Thus, the checkpoints of jj are {(1+δ)ρ′}ρ′≥ρj\{(1+\delta)^{\rho^{\prime}}\}_{\rho^{\prime}\geq\rho_{j}}, and job jj can reach a checkpoint at most ⌈log1+δ⁡(pj/p^j)⌉+1\lceil\log_{1+\delta}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})\rceil+1 times.

3.1 Algorithm: SNAP

Our algorithm, which we call Simulated Non-preemptive Adaptive Prediction (SNAP) algorithm, proceeds in epochs 1,2,…,K1,2,\dots,K. Epoch kk starts at time eke_{k} and ends at time ek+1e_{k+1}, at which point epoch k+1k+1 begins immediately. The first epoch starts at time e1=0e_{1}=0. At the start of epoch kk, let Jk:=J⁡(ek)J_{k}:=J(e_{k}) denote the set of available jobs for processing. Here, J⁡(t):={j∣rj≤t<Cj}J(t):=\{j\mid r_{j}\leq t<C_{j}\} is the set of jobs alive at time tt. Let nk:=|Jk|n_{k}:=|J_{k}|. Let β,γ∈(0,1)\beta,\gamma\in(0,1) be some constants that we optimize later.

At the beginning of each epoch, we compute a complete schedule for the duration of the epoch and follow it. Specifically, we execute the following steps:

  1. 1.

    Compute Proportional Fairness (PF) processing rates. We compute the PF rates for the set JkJ_{k}, denoted by y(k):=PF​(Jk)y^{(k)}:=\text{PF}(J_{k}). Formally, y(k)y^{(k)} is the solution to the following convex program with J=JkJ=J_{k}:

    PF(J):max\displaystyle\textrm{PF}(J):\quad\max ∑j∈Jlog⁡(yj)\displaystyle\sum_{j\in J}\log(y_{j})
    s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} ∑j∈Jxi​j≤1∀i∈M,∑i∈Mxi​j≤1,yj=∑i∈Mλi​j​xi​j\displaystyle\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}\leq 1\quad\forall i\in M,\quad\sum_{i\in M}x_{ij}\leq 1,\quad y_{j}=\sum_{i\in M}\lambda_{ij}x_{ij} j∈J,\displaystyle j\in J,
    xi​j≥0∀i∈M,j∈J.\displaystyle x_{ij}\geq 0\quad\forall i\in M,\ j\in J.

    This can be solved approximately in near linear time [CMP22].

  2. 2.

    Compute remaining requirement to the next checkpoint. For each job j∈Jkj\in J_{k}, we define the remaining processing requirement to reach its next checkpoint as uj,k:=(1+δ)h+1−qj​(ek)u_{j,k}:=(1+\delta)^{h+1}-q_{j}(e_{k}), where h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N} such that (1+δ)h≤max⁡{p^j,qj​(ek)}<(1+δ)h+1(1+\delta)^{h}\leq\max\{\hat{p}_{j},q_{j}(e_{k})\}<(1+\delta)^{h+1}.

  3. 3.

    Determine the simulation duration. Let lkl_{k} denote the length of the shortest time interval such that, if jobs are processed at rates y(k)y^{(k)} during the time interval, at least ⌈β​nk⌉\lceil\beta n_{k}\rceil jobs from JkJ_{k} reach their next checkpoint. Formally, let the jobs in JkJ_{k} be sorted in non-decreasing order of uj,k/yj(k)u_{j,k}/y^{(k)}_{j}. If j∗j^{*} is the ⌈β​nk⌉\lceil\beta n_{k}\rceil-th job in this ordering, breaking ties arbitrarily, then the duration is defined as lk=uj∗,k/yj∗(k)l_{k}=u_{j^{*},k}/y^{(k)}_{j^{*}}. The targeted processing requirement for each job j∈Jkj\in J_{k} in the current epoch is then vj,k=min⁡{uj,k,lk​yj(k)}v_{j,k}=\min\{u_{j,k},l_{k}y^{(k)}_{j}\}.

  4. 4.

    Convert to a non-preemptive schedule. Since the fractional assignments xi​jx_{ij} from Step 1 constitute a valid preemptive schedule for the required processing requirement vj,kv_{j,k}, we can construct a non-preemptive (and non-migratory) schedule that begins at time eke_{k} and completes by time ek+4⋅lke_{k}+4\cdot l_{k} where each each job j∈Jkj\in J_{k} is processed by vj,kv_{j,k} units [CSV12].

We note that the algorithm runs in polynomial time, as both the conversion method [CSV12] and the computation of PF rates [IKM18, JLM26] are polynomial-time solvable. From the description of SNAP, we can make the following two observations.

Observation 3.1.

In an epoch kk, at least ⌈β​nk⌉\lceil\beta n_{k}\rceil jobs reach a checkpoint.

Observation 3.2.

For each epoch kk, we have that ek+1−ek≤4⋅lke_{k+1}-e_{k}\leq 4\cdot l_{k}.

We first argue about the number of preemptions and migrations of SNAP.

Theorem 3.3.

When all job sizes are underestimated, the total number of preemptions performed by SNAP is at most O⁡(1β​δ​∑j(log2⁡pjp^j+1)).O\big(\frac{1}{\beta\delta}\sum_{j}\big(\log_{2}\frac{p_{j}}{\hat{p}_{j}}+1\big)\big).

Proof.

In each epoch kk, every job j∈Jkj\in J_{k} is preempted (or migrated) at most once due to the non-preemptive nature of the schedule constructed in Step 4. Thus, the total number of preemptions is bounded by ∑knk\sum_{k}n_{k}. By Observation 3.1, at least β​nk\beta n_{k} jobs reach a checkpoint during an epoch. Consequently, ∑knk≤1β×(Total number of exhaustions)\sum_{k}n_{k}\leq\frac{1}{\beta}\times(\text{Total number of exhaustions}). Each job jj can reach a checkpoint at most ⌈log1+δ⁡(pj/p^j)⌉+1\lceil\log_{1+\delta}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})\rceil+1 times (under the assumption of underestimated predictions). Therefore,

∑knk≤1β​∑j(⌈log1+δ⁡pjp^j⌉+1)=O⁡(1β​δ​∑j(1+log2⁡pjp^j)).∎\textstyle\sum_{k}n_{k}\hskip-1.42262pt\leq\hskip-1.42262pt\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{j}\bigl(\lceil\log_{1+\delta}\frac{p_{j}}{\hat{p}_{j}}\rceil\hskip-1.42262pt+\hskip-1.42262pt1\bigr)\hskip-1.42262pt=\hskip-1.42262ptO\bigl(\frac{1}{\beta\delta}\sum_{j}\bigl(1+\log_{2}\frac{p_{j}}{\hat{p}_{j}}\bigr)\bigr)\ .\qed

We next aim to prove the following theorem on SNAP’s competitive ratio.

Theorem 3.4.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, the SNAP algorithm with η=ε2​(1+ε)\eta=\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1+\varepsilon)} and β=ε24​(1+ε)​(2+ε)\beta=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{4(1+\varepsilon)(2+\varepsilon)}. achieves a total completion time that is at most 14.48​(1+ε)14.48(1+\varepsilon) times the optimum.

We split up the proof of this theorem into multiple lemmas. From now on fix the schedule of the SNAP algorithm. Let KK be the number of epochs. Let 𝖺𝗅𝗀⁡(p)\mathsf{alg}(p) denote SNAP’s total completion time objective for a processing time vector p={pj}jp=\{p_{j}\}_{j}.

Lemma 3.5.

It holds that 𝖺𝗅𝗀⁡(p)≤4​∑k=1Knk​lk\mathsf{alg}(p)\leq 4\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}l_{k}.

Proof.

We have

𝖺𝗅𝗀⁡(p)=∑k=1K∑t=ekek+1−1|J⁡(t)|≤∑k=1K∑t=ekek+1−1|J⁡(ek)|=∑k=1K(ek+1−ek)​nk≤4​∑k=1Klk​nk,\displaystyle\mathsf{alg}(p)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t=e_{k}}^{e_{k+1}-1}|J(t)|\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t=e_{k}}^{e_{k+1}-1}|J(e_{k})|=\sum_{k=1}^{K}(e_{k+1}-e_{k})n_{k}\leq 4\sum_{k=1}^{K}l_{k}n_{k}\ ,

where the equalities use that each alive job contributes 11 per timestep and nk=|J⁡(ek)|n_{k}=|J(e_{k})|, and the inequalities use monotonicity of |J⁡(t)||J(t)| and Observation 3.2. ∎

Let 𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(zj∣j∈S)\mathsf{opt}(z_{j}\mid j\in S) denote the minimum total completion time to complete a set of jobs SS, where job j∈Sj\in S has a size zjz_{j}. For the sake of analysis, consider a set of jobs where we have one job for each j∈Jkj\in J_{k}, but with a different size, lk​yj(k)l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}. Since yj(k)y_{j}^{(k)} is PF’s processing rate on jj when it runs on JkJ_{k}, PF will finish them with these hypothetical sizes exactly at the same time. Using Theorem 4.1 of [JLM26], which shows that PF achieves a competitive ratio of two when it completes all jobs with the same arrival time at the same time, we have the following claim.

Claim 3.6.

For each epoch kk, we have nk​lk≤2⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Jk)n_{k}l_{k}\leq 2\cdot\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in J_{k}).

Let XkX_{k} be the jobs exhausted during epoch kk, strictly before the end of the epoch. Let Yk:=Jk∖XkY_{k}:=J_{k}\setminus X_{k}. Note that |Yk|≥(1−β)​nk|Y_{k}|\geq(1-\beta)n_{k} because of the definition of the epoch. Our next goal is to bound the RHS of the inequality in Claim 3.6 by a linear combination of analogous quantities restricted to XkX_{k} and YkY_{k}, respectively. The proof is deferred to Appendix D.1.

Claim 3.7.

For each epoch kk and any η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), we have,

𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Jk)≤1η​𝗈𝗉𝗍​(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Xk)+11−η​𝗈𝗉𝗍​(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Yk).\displaystyle\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in J_{k})\leq\frac{1}{\eta}\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in X_{k})+\frac{1}{1-\eta}\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in Y_{k})\ .

The following lemma upper bounds the cost incurred by our algorithm during epoch kk by the cost that the optimal solution must pay for the processing performed on jobs that are not exhausted in the middle of the epoch. We defer to Appendix D.1 the proof of the following lemma, which follows by combining Claims 3.6 and 3.7 with |Xk|≤β​nk|X_{k}|\leq\beta n_{k}.

Lemma 3.8.

For each epoch kk, we have nk​lk≤2​η(η−2​β)​(1−η)⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Yk)n_{k}l_{k}\leq\frac{2\eta}{(\eta-2\beta)(1-\eta)}\cdot\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in Y_{k}).

We then show that {lk​y(k)}j∈Yk\{l_{k}y^{(k)}\}_{j\in Y_{k}} is a decomposition of the full instance.

Lemma 3.9.

For every job jj, it holds that ∑k:j∈Yklkyj(k)≤pj\sum_{k:j\in Y_{k}}l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\leq p_{j}.

Proof.

Fix a job jj. Consider an epoch kk with j∈Ykj\in Y_{k}. Since jj is not exhausted until epoch kk’s end time, it is processed by lk​yj(k)l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)} during the epoch. The sum of this quantity over all epochs kk with j∈Ykj\in Y_{k} cannot exceed jj’s size, pjp_{j}. ∎

We now employ the “decomposition” lemma, which follows from the super-additivity of the non-preemptive optimum for unrelated machine scheduling [JLM26] and the 1.811.81-gap between the preemptive and non-preemptive optima for the total (weighted) completion time objective [Sit17].

Lemma 3.10 (Lemma 4.5 in [JLM26]).

Consider any set of jobs SS where each job jj has a size pjp_{j}. For each j∈Sj\in S, let pj,κ′≥0p_{j,\kappa^{\prime}}\geq 0, 1≤κ′≤κ1\leq\kappa^{\prime}\leq\kappa, be such that ∑κ′=1κpj,k′≤pj\sum_{\kappa^{\prime}=1}^{\kappa}p_{j,k^{\prime}}\leq p_{j}. Then, we have ∑κ′=1κ𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(pj,κ′∣j∈S)≤1.81⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(pj∣j∈S)\sum_{\kappa^{\prime}=1}^{\kappa}\mathsf{opt}(p_{j,\kappa^{\prime}}\mid j\in S)\leq 1.81\cdot\mathsf{opt}(p_{j}\mid j\in S).

Lemmas 3.9 and  3.10 immediately yield the following.

Corollary 3.11.

It holds that ∑k=1K𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(lk​yj(k)|j∈Yk)≤1.81⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(p)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\,|\,j\in Y_{k})\leq 1.81\cdot\mathsf{opt}(p).

We are now ready to prove Theorem 3.4. Using Lemma 3.5, Lemma 3.8, and Corollary 3.11, we obtain

𝖺𝗅𝗀⁡(p)≤4​∑k=1Knk​lk\displaystyle\mathsf{alg}(p)\leq 4\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}l_{k} ≤4​(2​η(η−2​β)​(1−η))​∑k=1K𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Yk)\displaystyle\leq 4\big(\tfrac{2\eta}{(\eta-2\beta)(1-\eta)}\big)\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in Y_{k})
≤14.48​(η(η−2​β)​(1−η))⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(p).\displaystyle\leq 14.48\big(\tfrac{\eta}{(\eta-2\beta)(1-\eta)}\big)\cdot\mathsf{opt}(p)\kern 5.0pt.

Hence, 𝖺𝗅𝗀≤14.48⋅(1+ε)⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(p)\mathsf{alg}\leq 14.48\cdot(1+\varepsilon)\cdot\mathsf{opt}(p) using η=ε2​(1+ε)\eta=\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1+\varepsilon)} and β=ε24​(1+ε)​(2+ε)\beta=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{4(1+\varepsilon)(2+\varepsilon)}.

4 A general framework for PSP and malleable job scheduling

We next present a general framework for the Polytope Scheduling Problem (PSP) with parsimonious preemption, which encompasses various scheduling problems [IKM18, JLM26]. There are nn jobs j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n with processing requirements pjp_{j}. A feasible schedule selects over time for every time tt a processing rate yj​(t)y_{j}(t) for each active job j∈J⁡(t)j\in J(t) from a given downward-closed polytope 𝒫={y∈ℝ≥0n∣B​y≤1}\mathcal{P}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq 0}\mid By\leq\textsf{1}\} for some matrix B=[bd​j]∈ℝ≥0D×nB=[b_{dj}]\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times n}_{\geq 0}. Job jj completes when it has received pjp_{j} amount of processing, that is, its completion time CjC_{j} is the earliest point in time t′t^{\prime} such that ∫rjt′yj​(t)​𝑑t≥pj\int_{r_{j}}^{t^{\prime}}y_{j}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\geq p_{j}. The goal is to minimize the total completion time ∑jCj\sum_{j}C_{j}. We again make the assumption that all jobs are underpredicted; we can mitigate this assumption as in the previous sections.

The framework.

Our framework is a generalization of SNAP in (cf. Section 3). The main difference lies in Step 4, where we assume to be given a procedure to convert a rate schedule (a vector belonging to 𝒫\mathcal{P}) into a schedule with few preemptions.

Definition 4.1 (α\alpha-approximate O⁡(1)O(1)-preemptive schedule).

For a given PSP schedule of length ll with fixed allocation {yj}j∈J\{y_{j}\}_{j\in J}, an α\alpha-approximate O⁡(1)O(1)-preemptive schedule satisfies processing requirements {l​yj}j∈J\{ly_{j}\}_{j\in J}, has a makespan of at most α​l\alpha l, and uses only O⁡(1)O(1) preemptions per job.

The definition of preemption depends on the specific PSP, as each polytope 𝒫\mathcal{P} determines a distinct scheduling problem. Consequently, Definition 4.1 allows us to reason within the abstract setting of the PSP, providing a general framework for our analysis. We again assume that all pjp_{j}’s are powers of 1+δ1+\delta for some constant δ>0\delta>0, which increases the competitive ratio by at most a factor of 1+δ1+\delta.

Our framework generalizes the SNAP algorithm. Thus, we focus here on the key modifications and defer the full description to Appendix E. The primary distinction lies in Step 4, which is adapted as follows: we compute an α\alpha-approximate O⁡(1)O(1)-preemptive schedule (as per Definition 4.1) for the set of jobs JkJ_{k}. For each job j∈Jkj\in J_{k}, the processing targets are defined as vj,k=min⁡{uj,k,lk​yj(k)}v_{j,k}=\min\{u_{j,k},l_{k}y^{(k)}_{j}\}. This schedule starts at time eke_{k} and is guaranteed to finish no later than ek+1≤ek+α​lke_{k+1}\leq e_{k}+\alpha l_{k}.

Analysis.

Bounding the number of preemptions is analogous to Theorem 3.3 (see Theorem E.1). For the analysis of the competitive ratio, for convenience we analyze our algorithm before the conversion to the α\alpha-approximate O⁡(1)O(1)-preemptive schedule, which we will call the virtual algorithm; in this case, we effectively have ek+1=ek+lke_{k+1}=e_{k}+l_{k}. This assumption does not alter the processing each job receives within an epoch. However, the conversion increases each job’s completion time by a factor of at most α\alpha, resulting in a multiplicative loss in the competitive ratio by a factor of α\alpha.

The primary departure from the analysis of SNAP for unrelated machines is that PSP lacks the super-additivity guarantees for subinstances (cf. Lemma 3.10). Consequently, we must use different techniques to bound the objective. Our main technical novelty is the introduction of a robust variant of PSP, which we term β\beta-robust PSP, and a corresponding analysis of PF within this framework.

Definition 4.2.

In the β\beta-robust PSP problem, we are given a PSP instance and a constant β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1). At any time tt, an algorithm selects a processing allocation y⁡(t)∈𝒫y(t)\in\mathcal{P} for the set of active jobs J⁡(t)J(t). An adversary then chooses a subset N⁡(t)⊆J⁡(t)N(t)\subseteq J(t) of at most β​|J⁡(t)|\beta|J(t)| jobs whose processing rates are nullified. Formally, the resulting processing allocation is: y^j(t):=yj(t)⋅1[j∉N(t)].\hat{y}_{j}(t):=y_{j}(t)\cdot\textsf{1}[j\notin N(t)].

We show in Appendix G the following theorem.

Theorem 4.3.

For any β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), PF is 27/(1−β)327/(1-\beta)^{3}-competitive for β\beta-robust PSP.

The key observation is that the schedule of the virtual algorithm can be interpreted as a schedule of PF for β\beta-robust PSP with a specific choice of the set of nullified jobs. Using this observation, we show in Appendix E that the virtual algorithm achieves a total completion time at most 27​(1+δ)(1−β)327\frac{(1+\delta)}{(1-\beta)^{3}} times the optimum. Setting δ=(1+ε)​(1−β)3−1\delta=(1+\varepsilon)(1-\beta)^{3}-1 and β=1−((1+δ)/(1+ε))1/3\beta=1-((1+\delta)/(1+\varepsilon))^{1/3} yields:

Theorem 4.4.

Given a procedure for computing α\alpha-approximate O⁡(1)O(1)-preemptive schedules, there exists a 27​α​(1+ε)27\alpha(1+\varepsilon)-competitive algorithm for PSP that performs at most O⁡(1ε3​∑j(1+log2⁡pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}\sum_{j}(1+\log_{2}p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) preemptions for any ε>0\varepsilon>0.

Finally, we can apply this theorem to malleable job scheduling on unrelated machines. Details are deferred to Appendix F.

Theorem 4.5.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is a 27​ee−1​(1+ε)27\frac{e}{e-1}(1+\varepsilon)-competitive algorithm that incurs at most O⁡(1ε3​∑j(1+log2⁡pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}\sum_{j}(1+\log_{2}p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) preemptions for minimizing the total completion time of malleable jobs on unrelated machines with non-decreasing, concave, and non-decreasing work speed-up functions.

5 Experiments

To the best of our knowledge, no existing algorithms limit preemption using predictions while simultaneously optimizing for the total completion time objective. To address this gap, we developed and implemented a suite of algorithms, including SNAP. With the exception of the Blind strategy, all of these algorithms incorporate novel algorithmic aspects. We use a default value of δ=1\delta=1. For additional implementation details, see Appendix I.1.

SNAP: Our primary algorithm, modified to eliminate idle time by running PMLF on each machine until a β\beta fraction of jobs are exhausted. Specifically, we follow Step 4 to assign jobs to machines in an epoch, which are then processed by PMLF on each machine. Doubling: A variant of the immediate-dispatch algorithm in [AGK12] (where each machine runs SJF and new jobs are assigned to minimize the marginal increase of the objective). This variant doubles a job’s estimated size whenever processing exceeds the current estimate and re-dispatches it to the machine that minimizes the objective increase. Blind: Based on the immediate-dispatch and non-migratory algorithm in [AGK12], this strategy is executed by assuming pj=p^jp_{j}=\hat{p}_{j} for all jobs. This algorithm makes no preemptions. Hybrid SNAP: A modified SNAP algorithm that begins with Doubling with large milestones {c​(1+δ)i​p^j∣i≥1}\{c(1+\delta)^{i}\hat{p}_{j}\mid i\geq 1\} for a large parameter c≥10c\geq 10 (to emulate the Blind strategy). Jobs that have reached several milestones are processed by SNAP.

Setup: We evaluated the algorithms on synthetic instances with m=10m=10 machines and n=100n=100 jobs. To model heterogeneity, 20% of jobs are designated as “special” (pj∼𝒰⁡[1,200]p_{j}\sim\mathcal{U}[1,200]) and are restricted to 2 specific machines, while regular jobs (pj∼𝒰⁡[1,10]p_{j}\sim\mathcal{U}[1,10]) can utilize any resource. Intuitively, special jobs represent tasks with large processing requirements that require specific hardware. (For other percentages of special jobs and machines we obtain similar results; see Appendix I).

The prediction error is controlled via a parameter R≥1R\geq 1; we set p^j=⌈pj/ξj⌉\hat{p}_{j}=\lceil p_{j}/\xi_{j}\rceil where ξj∼𝒰⁡[1,R]\xi_{j}\sim\mathcal{U}[1,R]. We evaluate the algorithms based on the total completion time objective normalized to the optimum (the competitive ratio) and the average number of preemptions per job. Comparisons are performed across exponentially increasing values of RR. We note that large prediction errors are common in practice [Par+18, Lei+15]; in particular, even top-tier database systems routinely misestimate join sizes, which directly dictate execution runtimes, by factors of 10001000 or more.

Results: Our experiments demonstrate that SNAP requires considerably fewer preemptions while effectively optimizing total completion time, particularly when prediction errors are large. These findings are summarized in Figure 1. Our main observations are as follows:

  • •

    Our results show that we can effectively leverage the highly preemptive PF algorithm to derive a preemption-parsimonious algorithm like SNAP. SNAP incurs fewer preemptions than natural benchmarks such as Doubling.

  • •

    It is known that Blind is 4-competitive if all predictions are accurate [AGK12], but its competitive ratio degrades linearly with error. Thus, Blind performs well for small RR but becomes impractical as RR increases.

  • •

    To achieve the “best of both worlds”, we implemented Hybrid SNAP. This approach yields promising results, consistently outperforming or matching others in both the objective value and in minimizing preemptions.

Further experimental results, including a detailed analysis of the tradeoff between the competitive ratio and preemptions as a function of δ\delta, are deferred to Appendix I.

6 Conclusions

In this work, we presented the first analytical study of the trade-off between job latency minimization and preemption overhead in online scheduling with predictions. By leveraging machine-learned predictions, our SNAP and PMLF algorithms avoid the excessive preemption required by classical non-clairvoyant algorithms. We proved that these algorithms are constant-competitive in various environments, including single, identical, and unrelated machines, with preemption costs that scale logarithmically with the prediction error. Our experiments show that SNAP remains stable in minimizing both preemption overhead and total completion time, and also demonstrate the favorable performance of the other heuristics developed in this study.

Future research could further explore hybridizing the Blind and SNAP frameworks. This approach seeks to leverage the efficiency of Blind under accurate predictions while maintaining the robustness of SNAP in the presence of large errors, effectively bridging the gap between optimistic performance and worst-case reliability.

Appendix A Lower bounds

A.1 General lower bound on the number of preemptions

For a fixed algorithm, let 𝖯𝖬⁡(x)\mathsf{PM}(x) denote the maximum number of preemptions that the algorithm makes on a job of size xx. The following theorem was originally stated and proven by Motwani et al. [MPT94]. We give a more detailed proof for completeness and clarity.

Theorem A.1 ([MPT94]).

Consider a non-clairvoyant algorithm that preempts a job of size xx at most 𝖯𝖬⁡(x)\mathsf{PM}(x) times. If 𝖯𝖬⁡(x)=o⁡(log⁡x)\mathsf{PM}(x)=o(\log x), then for every n≥2n\geq 2 there exists an instance with nn jobs on which the algorithm has a competitive ratio of at least n/2n/2.

Proof.

Let B:=2​n2B:=2n^{2} and m=B2​nm=B^{2n}. Since logm⁡x=log⁡x/log⁡m\log_{m}x=\log x/\log m, there exists a sufficiently large x0x_{0} such that for every x≥x0x\geq x_{0} we have 𝖯𝖬⁡(x)≤logm⁡x\mathsf{PM}(x)\leq\log_{m}x, and additionally we can assume that x0=BK+1x_{0}=B^{K+1} for some integer K≥2K\geq 2.

Consider an instance on nn jobs, each of size x0x_{0}, and the algorithm’s schedule at time t=x0t=x_{0}. Note that before this time, the algorithm cannot complete any job. By our assumption, the total number of preemptions until time tt can be at most

n⋅logm⁡x0=n⋅logB2​n⁡BK+1=n⋅K+12​n=K+12<K,n\cdot\log_{m}x_{0}=n\cdot\log_{B^{2n}}B^{K+1}=n\cdot\frac{K+1}{2n}=\frac{K+1}{2}<K\ ,

because K≥2K\geq 2.

Now, partition the time interval [1,BK]⊆[0,x0][1,B^{K}]\subseteq[0,x_{0}] into KK intervals Ii=[Bi−1,Bi)I_{i}=[B^{i-1},B^{i}) for i=1,…,Ki=1,\ldots,K. Since there are KK intervals before time tt but less than KK preemptions, by the pigeonhole principle, there must be at least one interval IiI_{i} that contains no preemption. Fix such an interval IiI_{i} and let jj be the job that is processed during IiI_{i}. Note that during IiI_{i}, job jj receives a total processing of at least Bi−Bi−1=(B−1)⋅Bi−1=(2​n2−1)⋅Bi−1B^{i}-B^{i-1}=(B-1)\cdot B^{i-1}=(2n^{2}-1)\cdot B^{i-1}. Let ej′​(Bi)e_{j^{\prime}}(B^{i}) denote the amount of processing that job j′j^{\prime} received until time BiB^{i}. Note that ej′​(Bi)≥(2​n2−1)⋅Bi−1e_{j^{\prime}}(B^{i})\geq(2n^{2}-1)\cdot B^{i-1}, and for every job j′≠jj^{\prime}\neq j we have ej′​(Bi)≤Bi−1e_{j^{\prime}}(B^{i})\leq B^{i-1}.

We next define a new instance with the same set of jobs, but with processing times

  • •

    pj=ej​(Bi)p_{j}=e_{j}(B^{i}) and

  • •

    pj′=ej′​(Bi)+εp_{j^{\prime}}=e_{j^{\prime}}(B^{i})+\varepsilon for all j′≠jj^{\prime}\neq j, where ε=Bi−12​n2\varepsilon=\frac{B^{i-1}}{2n^{2}}.

By construction and the fact that the algorithm is deterministic, observe that no job completes before time BiB^{i}. Moreover, job jj completes exactly at time BiB^{i}.

We compute a lower bound on the competitive ratio of the algorithm on this instance. Note that Cj≥Cj′C_{j}\geq C_{j^{\prime}} for all j′≠jj^{\prime}\neq j. Hence,

𝖺𝗅𝗀≥n​Cj≥n⋅pj.\mathsf{alg}\geq nC_{j}\geq n\cdot p_{j}\ .

We next give an upper bound on the optimal objective value. Note that for every job j′≠jj^{\prime}\neq j, we have

n2​pj′≤n2​(Bi−1+Bi−12​n2)=n2​Bi−1+Bi−12≤(2​n2−1)⋅Bi−1≤pj.n^{2}p_{j^{\prime}}\leq n^{2}\left(B^{i-1}+\frac{B^{i-1}}{2n^{2}}\right)=n^{2}B^{i-1}+\frac{B^{i-1}}{2}\leq(2n^{2}-1)\cdot B^{i-1}\leq p_{j}\ .

Let p=pj/n2p=p_{j}/n^{2}. Scheduling job jj last achieves a total completion time of at most

(n−1)​n2​p+(n−1)​p+pj≤n2​p+pj≤2​pj.\frac{(n-1)n}{2}p+(n-1)p+p_{j}\leq n^{2}p+p_{j}\leq 2p_{j}\ .

Thus,

𝖺𝗅𝗀𝗈𝗉𝗍≥n⋅pj2​pj=n2,\frac{\mathsf{alg}}{\mathsf{opt}}\geq\frac{n\cdot p_{j}}{2p_{j}}=\frac{n}{2}\ ,

which completes the proof. ∎

Theorem A.2.

If for each job jj it holds that p^j≤pj≤λj​p^j\hat{p}_{j}\leq p_{j}\leq\lambda_{j}\hat{p}_{j} and there exists a job jj such that the algorithm preempts jj at most o⁡(log⁡λj)o(\log\lambda_{j}), then the algorithm has a competitive ratio of at least Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) for sufficiently large λ\lambda and nn.

Proof.

Follows directly from the proof of Theorem A.1 by setting p^j=1\hat{p}_{j}=1 for all jobs jj. This makes the jobs indistinguishable and the proof strategy applicable. Moreover, λj=pj/p^j=pj\lambda_{j}=p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j}=p_{j} for all jobs jj, hence the guarantees translate. ∎

A.2 Trade-off lower bound

Theorem A.3.

If a deterministic learning-augmented algorithm uses at most ss preemptions in total for a correctly predicted instance with nn jobs, then there exists an instance where every job is overestimated and the algorithm has a competitive ratio of at least Ω⁡((n−s)/s)\Omega((n-s)/s).

Proof.

Let p^j=pj=P\hat{p}_{j}=p_{j}=P for all jobs j∈Jj\in J be the correctly predicted instance with nn jobs. Consider the schedule of the fixed deterministic algorithm on this instance. Until time PP, the algorithm cannot have completed any job. Assume that until time PP, the algorithm does at most ss preemptions, hence the algorithm can touch at most s+1s+1 jobs until time PP. Let ZZ denote the set of jobs that were not touched by the algorithm until time PP, and note that |Z|≥n−(s+1)|Z|\geq n-(s+1). For each job j∈J∖Zj\in J\setminus Z, denote by qjq_{j} the amount of work done by the algorithm on jj until time PP.

We now construct another instance as follows. We set p^j=P\hat{p}_{j}=P for all j∈Jj\in J and

pj={1if ​j∈Zqj+εif ​j∈J∖Zp_{j}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }j\in Z\\ q_{j}+\varepsilon&\text{if }j\in J\setminus Z\end{cases}

Since the algorithm is deterministic, it behaves the same on this new instance as on the original instance, because with the same schedule as before it again will not complete any job until time PP. Thus, 𝖺𝗅𝗀≥P⋅|Z|\mathsf{alg}\geq P\cdot|Z| for this instance. However, an optimal solution can schedule all short jobs in ZZ first, and then schedule the long jobs in J∖ZJ\setminus Z in any order. This gives 𝗈𝗉𝗍≤|Z|​(|Z|+1)2+(n−|Z|)​(|Z|+P+n​ε)\mathsf{opt}\leq\frac{|Z|(|Z|+1)}{2}+(n-|Z|)(|Z|+P+n\varepsilon). By choosing P≥n3P\geq n^{3}, we conclude that

𝖺𝗅𝗀𝗈𝗉𝗍≥P⋅|Z||Z|​(|Z|+1)2+(n−|Z|)​(|Z|+P+n​ε)≥P⋅(n−(s+1))n2+(s+1)​(n+P+n​ε)≥Ω⁡(n−ss).\frac{\mathsf{alg}}{\mathsf{opt}}\geq\frac{P\cdot|Z|}{\frac{|Z|(|Z|+1)}{2}+(n-|Z|)(|Z|+P+n\varepsilon)}\geq\frac{P\cdot(n-(s+1))}{n^{2}+(s+1)(n+P+n\varepsilon)}\geq\Omega\left(\frac{n-s}{s}\right)\ .

This completes the proof of the theorem. ∎

Appendix B Single machine

B.1 Analysis of PMLF

We present the full proof of Theorem 2.1.

See 2.1

Proof.

We first bound the number of preemptions. Note that jj is only preempted when it is moved between queues. Since job jj starts in Qk′Q_{k^{\prime}} where (1+δ)k′≤p^j<(1+δ)k′+1(1+\delta)^{k^{\prime}}\leq\hat{p}_{j}<(1+\delta)^{k^{\prime}+1} and completes in QkQ_{k} where (1+δ)k≤pj<(1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k}\leq p_{j}<(1+\delta)^{k+1}, it is moved at most k−k′+1=O⁡(log1+δ⁡(pj/p^j))=O⁡(1δ​log2⁡(pj/p^j))k-k^{\prime}+1=O(\log_{1+\delta}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j}))=O(\frac{1}{\delta}\log_{2}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) times across queues.

We next prove an upper bound on the competitive ratio, for which we use a classic delay decomposition [MPT94]. Fix a job jj with (1+δ)k≤pj<(1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k}\leq p_{j}<(1+\delta)^{k+1} and let CjC_{j} denote its completion time. Note that at the completion time CjC_{j}, it belongs to queue QkQ_{k}. Let d⁡(i,j)d(i,j) denote the total delay that job ii causes to job jj, which is the total amount of work done on ii before time CjC_{j}. Clearly, d⁡(i,j)≤pid(i,j)\leq p_{i}. Moreover, since jj completes at time CjC_{j} while belonging to queue QkQ_{k}, the algorithm can only work on ii before CjC_{j} whenever ii belongs to a queue Qk′Q_{k^{\prime}} with k′≤kk^{\prime}\leq k. This implies d⁡(i,j)<(1+δ)k+1d(i,j)<(1+\delta)^{k+1}. Thus, d⁡(i,j)≤min⁡{pi,(1+δ)k+1}d(i,j)\leq\min\{p_{i},(1+\delta)^{k+1}\}, which is at most (1+δ)​min⁡{pi,pj}(1+\delta)\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\} because pj≥(1+δ)kp_{j}\geq(1+\delta)^{k}. Since our algorithm does not idle,

Cj≤∑i=1nd⁡(i,j)≤(1+δ)​∑i=1nmin⁡{pi,pj}.C_{j}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(i,j)\leq(1+\delta)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\}\ .

Summing over all jobs jj gives

∑j=1nCj≤(1+δ)​∑j=1n∑i=1nmin⁡{pi,pj}≤(1+δ)⋅2​𝗈𝗉𝗍,\sum_{j=1}^{n}C_{j}\leq(1+\delta)\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\}\leq(1+\delta)\cdot 2\mathsf{opt}\ ,

where the second inequality follows the fact that scheduling jobs in non-decreasing order of their processing times is optimal [Smi56], thus, 𝗈𝗉𝗍=∑jpj+∑j=1n∑i>jnmin⁡{pi,pj}\mathsf{opt}=\sum_{j}p_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i>j}^{n}\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\}. ∎

B.2 Job arrival over time

We next show how PMLF and its analysis in the proof of Theorem 2.1 can be generalized to the setting with online arrival of jobs. In this setting, a job jj arrives at its release time rj≥0r_{j}\geq 0, and an online algorithm does not know about jj’s existence before that time. PMLF can be extended in a straightforward way to this dynamic scenario:

  • •

    Maintain a set of FIFO queues {Q0,Q1,…}\{Q_{0},Q_{1},\ldots\}.

  • •

    Whenever a job jj with prediction p^j\hat{p}_{j} arrives, we push it into queue QkQ_{k} where (1+δ)k≤p^j≤(1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k}\leq\hat{p}_{j}\leq(1+\delta)^{k+1}.

  • •

    At any time tt, work on the front job of the non-empty queue of the lowest index.

  • •

    If a job j∈Qij\in Q_{i} has received a total processing equal to (1+δ)i+1(1+\delta)^{i+1}, move it from QiQ_{i} to the end of Qi+1Q_{i+1}.

We prove the following theorem.

Theorem B.1.

For any constant δ>0\delta>0, PMLF is (3+2​δ)(3+2\delta)-competitive for minimizing the total completion time on a single machine with online job arrival and performs at most O⁡(1δ​log2⁡(pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\delta}\log_{2}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) preemptions for each job jj if there are only underpredictions.

Proof.

The proof for the bound on the number of preemption is the same as for Theorem 2.1.

We next prove an upper bound on the competitive ratio, for which we use a classic delay decomposition [MPT94]. Fix a job jj with (1+δ)k≤pj<(1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k}\leq p_{j}<(1+\delta)^{k+1} and let CjC_{j} denote its completion time. Note that at the completion time CjC_{j}, it belongs to queue QkQ_{k}. Let d⁡(i,j)d(i,j) denote the total delay that job ii causes to job jj after jj has been released, which is the total amount of work done on ii between times rjr_{j} and CjC_{j}. Clearly, d⁡(i,j)≤pid(i,j)\leq p_{i}. Moreover, since jj completes at time CjC_{j} while belonging to queue QkQ_{k}, the algorithm can only work on ii during [rj,Cj][r_{j},C_{j}] whenever ii belongs to a queue Qk′Q_{k^{\prime}} with k′≤kk^{\prime}\leq k. This implies d⁡(i,j)<(1+δ)k+1d(i,j)<(1+\delta)^{k+1}. Thus, d⁡(i,j)≤min⁡{pi,(1+δ)k+1}d(i,j)\leq\min\{p_{i},(1+\delta)^{k+1}\}, which is at most (1+δ)​min⁡{pi,pj}(1+\delta)\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\} because pj≥(1+δ)kp_{j}\geq(1+\delta)^{k}. Since our algorithm does not idle unnecessarily, we have

Cj≤rj+∑i=1nd⁡(i,j)≤rj+(1+δ)​∑i=1nmin⁡{pi,pj}.C_{j}\leq r_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(i,j)\leq r_{j}+(1+\delta)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\}\ .

Summing over all jobs jj gives

∑j=1nCj≤∑j=1nrj+(1+δ)​∑j=1n∑i=1nmin⁡{pi,pj}≤𝗈𝗉𝗍+(1+δ)⋅2​𝗈𝗉𝗍,\sum_{j=1}^{n}C_{j}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n}r_{j}+(1+\delta)\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\}\leq\mathsf{opt}+(1+\delta)\cdot 2\mathsf{opt}\ ,

where the second inequality uses

  • •

    that scheduling jobs in non-decreasing order of their processing times is optimal [Smi56], thus, 𝗈𝗉𝗍=∑jpj+∑j=1n∑i>jnmin⁡{pi,pj}\mathsf{opt}=\sum_{j}p_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i>j}^{n}\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\}, and

  • •

    ∑j=1nrj≤𝗈𝗉𝗍\sum_{j=1}^{n}r_{j}\leq\mathsf{opt} is a trivial lower bound.

This completes the proof of the theorem. ∎

B.3 Weakly enforcing underestimations

In this section, we prove Theorem 2.2, which we first restate for convenience.

See 2.2

Proof.

Let JuJ^{u} and JoJ^{o} be the set of overestimated and underestimated jobs. Note that |Jo|≤g|J^{o}|\leq g. Let nu​(t)n^{u}(t) be the number of underestimated unfinished jobs at time tt, and n⁡(t)n(t) be the total number of unfinished jobs at time tt. Thus, n⁡(t)≥g/γ≥(n⁡(t)−nu​(t))/γn(t)\geq g/\gamma\geq(n(t)-n^{u}(t))/\gamma for every time t≤Tt\leq T. Now we can compute

𝖺𝗅𝗀=∫0∞n⁡(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\mathsf{alg}=\int_{0}^{\infty}n(t)\,dt =∫0Tnu​(t)​𝑑t+∫0T(n⁡(t)−nu​(t))​𝑑t+∫T∞n⁡(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}n^{u}(t)\,dt+\int_{0}^{T}(n(t)-n^{u}(t))\,dt+\int_{T}^{\infty}n(t)\,dt
≤∫0Tnu​(t)​𝑑t+∫0Tγ​n​(t)​𝑑t+∫T∞n⁡(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{T}n^{u}(t)\,dt+\int_{0}^{T}\gamma n(t)\,dt+\int_{T}^{\infty}n(t)\,dt
≤∫0Tnu​(t)​𝑑t+γ​𝖺𝗅𝗀+∫T∞n⁡(t)​𝑑t.\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{T}n^{u}(t)\,dt+\gamma\mathsf{alg}+\int_{T}^{\infty}n(t)\,dt\ .

Hence,

(1−γ)​𝖺𝗅𝗀\displaystyle(1-\gamma)\mathsf{alg} ≤∫0Tnu​(t)​𝑑t+∫T∞n⁡(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{T}n^{u}(t)\,dt+\int_{T}^{\infty}n(t)\,dt
≤∑j∈JuCj+∑j∈Jo(Cj−T),\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j\in J^{u}}C_{j}+\sum_{j\in J^{o}}(C_{j}-T)\ , (1)

where the last inequality uses the fact that each job j∈Juj\in J^{u} is counted in both nu​(t)n^{u}(t) and n⁡(t)n(t), and each job j∈Joj\in J^{o} is only counted in n⁡(t)n(t) and not in nu​(t)n^{u}(t). We can now consider both sums individually.

For every underestimated job j∈Juj\in J^{u}, we can use the same proof as in the proof of Theorem 2.1. Before jj’s completion, it can only be delayed by jobs ii that are in queues of index at most ⌊log1+δ⁡pj⌋\lfloor\log_{1+\delta}p_{j}\rfloor, hence ii delays jj by at most min⁡{pi,(1+δ)​pj}\min\{p_{i},(1+\delta)p_{j}\} many times. Thus,

Cj≤∑i∈Jmin⁡{pi,(1+δ)​pj}.C_{j}\leq\sum_{i\in J}\min\{p_{i},(1+\delta)p_{j}\}\ .

For every overestimated job j∈Joj\in J^{o}, we can also use the same argumentation but only for delays that happen after time TT. This gives

Cj−T≤∑i∈Jmin⁡{pi,(1+δ)​pj}.C_{j}-T\leq\sum_{i\in J}\min\{p_{i},(1+\delta)p_{j}\}\ .

Combining both bounds implies that (1) is at most

(1+δ)​∑j∈J∑i∈Jmin⁡{pi,pj}≤(1+δ)​2⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍.(1+\delta)\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{i\in J}\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\}\leq(1+\delta)2\cdot\mathsf{opt}\ .

Thus, 𝖺𝗅𝗀≤1+δ1−γ⋅2⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍=2​(1+ε)⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍\mathsf{alg}\leq\frac{1+\delta}{1-\gamma}\cdot 2\cdot\mathsf{opt}=2(1+\varepsilon)\cdot\mathsf{opt} by choosing δ=ε2\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{2} and γ=ε2​(1+ε)\gamma=\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1+\varepsilon)}.

We next bound the number of preemptions. For underpredicted jobs the same bound as in Theorem 2.1 applies for all preemptions before time TT. At time TT, each unfinished job is reinserted at most once, and after time TT, each job is preempted at most O⁡(log1+δ⁡pj)O(\log_{1+\delta}p_{j}). Hence, the total number of preemptions is at most

O⁡(1δ​∑j∈Jlog⁡pjp^j+gγ​δ​log⁡pmax),O\bigg(\frac{1}{\delta}\sum_{j\in J}\log\frac{p_{j}}{\hat{p}_{j}}+\frac{g}{\gamma\delta}\log p_{\max}\bigg)\ ,

which implies the stated bound for our choice of δ\delta and γ\gamma. ∎

Appendix C Scheduling on identical parallel machines

In this section, we show that our single machine algorithm PMLF can be extended to scheduling on mm parallel identical machines. We first restate the generalization of PMLF for identical parallel machines. Let δ>0\delta>0 be a constant.

  • •

    Maintain a set of queues {Q0,Q1,…}\{Q_{0},Q_{1},\ldots\}. Initially, place a job jj with (1+δ)k≤p^j<(1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k}\leq\hat{p}_{j}<(1+\delta)^{k+1} into QkQ_{k}.

  • •

    At any time tt, for each available job jj, let (k,a)(k,a) be the tuple where kk is the index of jj’s current queue, and aa is its position in that queue, where the head of the queue has position 11. Let ⪯\preceq denote the total over all available jobs that corresponds to the lexicographic order of those tuples. Schedule the first at most mm jobs of ⪯\preceq.

  • •

    If a job j∈Qij\in Q_{i} has received a total processing equal to (1+δ)i+1(1+\delta)^{i+1} at time tt, remove it from QiQ_{i} and place it at the end of Qi+1Q_{i+1}.

We show the following theorem, which matches the guarantees of our single machine result given in Theorem 2.1.

Theorem C.1.

For the setting of only underestimated predictions, PMLF is (2+2​δ)(2+2\delta)-competitive for minimizing the total completion time on parallel identical machines and performs at most O⁡(1δ​∑jlog⁡(pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\delta}\sum_{j}\log(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) preemptions.

We split the proof of this theorem into two lemmas. We first bound the number of preemptions, which is equivalent to the argument in the proof of Theorem 2.1.

Lemma C.2.

For the setting of only underestimated predictions, PMLF uses at most O⁡(1δ​∑jlog⁡(pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\delta}\sum_{j}\log(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) preemptions on mm parallel identical machines.

Proof.

We first argue about the number of preemptions, which is equivalent to the argument in the proof of Theorem 2.1. Note that jj is only preempted when it is moved between queues. Since job jj starts in Qk′Q_{k^{\prime}} where (1+δ)k′≤p^j<(1+δ)k′+1(1+\delta)^{k^{\prime}}\leq\hat{p}_{j}<(1+\delta)^{k^{\prime}+1} and completes in QkQ_{k} where (1+δ)k≤pj<(1+δ)k+1(1+\delta)^{k}\leq p_{j}<(1+\delta)^{k+1}, it is moved at most k−k′+1=O⁡(log1+δ⁡(pj/p^j))k-k^{\prime}+1=O(\log_{1+\delta}(p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) often. ∎

For proving the bound on the competitive ratio, we require the following mixed lower bound.

For the problem of minimizing the total completion time of nn jobs on mm identical parallel machines, given a partition pj=pj(1)+pj(2)p_{j}=p_{j}^{(1)}+p_{j}^{(2)} for each job jj, it holds that

𝗈𝗉𝗍≥12​m​∑j=1n∑i=1nmin⁡{pi(1),pj(1)}+∑j=1npj(2).\mathsf{opt}\geq\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{p^{(1)}_{i},p^{(1)}_{j}\}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_{j}^{(2)}\ .

D.2 Job arrival over time: sketch

We now discuss how to extend our algorithm and analysis for unrelated machines to accommodate jobs arriving over time. We note that we do not optimize the parameters introduced here, specifically ν\nu. For convenience we will set ν=2​β\nu=2\beta. Furthermore, while we detail the necessary algorithmic changes and address the subtle points of the analysis, we provide only a compact proof sketch. As discussed in the introduction, this follows our primary focus, which remains on settings where jobs do not arrive over time.

Algorithmically, since our approach simulates the PF schedule within each epoch using a non-preemptive schedule, we should refine epochs whenever a significant number of new jobs arrives. Specifically, we initiate a sub-epoch if the number of new arrivals reaches a ν\nu-fraction of the currently active jobs: if J⁡(ek)J(e_{k}) denotes the set of jobs present at the beginning of epoch kk, the first sub-epoch (if it exists) begins at time ek,1e_{k,1} when ν​|J⁡(ek)|\nu|J(e_{k})| new jobs have arrived while the non-preemptive PF-simulated schedule (Step 4) is being executed. In general, if J⁡(ek,h)J(e_{k,h}) are the jobs alive at the start of the hhth sub-epoch, then the (h+1)(h+1)th sub-epoch begins at time ek,h+1e_{k,h+1} when ν​|J⁡(ek,h)|\nu|J(e_{k,h})| new jobs have arrived while the non-preemptive PF-simulated schedule (Step 4) of the hhth sub-epoch is being executed.

We note that from an algorithmic standpoint, epochs and sub-epochs are identical; this distinction is maintained primarily for the purpose of analysis.

Bounding preemptions.

We first discuss how we can upper bound the number of preemptions. If an epoch kk has no sub-epochs, then the analysis proceeds as before as the newly arriving jobs are not preempted. So, suppose it has sub-epochs, 1,2,…,h,…,H1,2,\ldots,h,\ldots,H. The additional preemptions initiated at the beginning of each sub-epoch, that is at time ek,he_{k,h}, can be charged to the new jobs arriving during (ek,h−1,ek,h](e_{k,h-1},e_{k,h}]. Here, for convenience, ek,0:=eke_{k,0}:=e_{k}. Note that because each arrival is responsible for at most 1/ν1/\nu jobs in this charging scheme and is charged only once during its lifetime, the scheme is valid.

Bounding total completion time.

We now focus on bounding the total completion time objective. To this end, consider a fixed epoch kk. First suppose it contains no sub-epochs. Recall that the cost of each epoch is bounded by 4​nk​lk4n_{k}l_{k}, where nk:=|J⁡(ek)|n_{k}:=|J(e_{k})| and 4​lk4l_{k} represents an upper bound on the epoch’s length. Since the additional arrivals (up to ν​nk\nu n_{k} jobs) cannot be processed until time eke_{k}, the optimal solution must also wait, just as our algorithm does, thereby incurring a comparable cost. During the epoch, the additional cost incurred is at most 4​ν​nk​lk4\nu n_{k}l_{k}. Consequently, this increases the objective by a factor of at most 1+ν1+\nu.

We now consider the more interesting case where the fixed epoch kk contains sub-epochs. For easy notation, let th:=ek,ht_{h}:=e_{k,h} and t0:=ekt_{0}:=e_{k}. Similarly, J0:=J⁡(ek)J_{0}:=J(e_{k}), and Jh:=J⁡(ek,h)J_{h}:=J(e_{k,h}). Also, for simplicity, we call the time interval [t0,t1)[t_{0},t_{1}) as the 00th epoch. Let tH+1t_{H+1} denote the last epoch’s end time.

Since we set ν=2​β\nu=2\beta, less than ν/2\nu/2 fraction of jobs reach their checkpoints, meaning that at most ν/2\nu/2 fraction of jobs can be completed; yet ν\nu fraction of jobs newly arrive. Thus, it follows that |Jh+1|≥(1+ν/2)​|Jh||J_{h+1}|\geq(1+\nu/2)|J_{h}| for all h=0,1,…,H−1h=0,1,\ldots,H-1. We charge the cost of jobs that were alive at any point during [e0,eH−2)[e_{0},e_{H-2}), denoted as the set V1V_{1}, up until time tH−1t_{H-1} to the arrival times of the jobs arriving in the penultimate epoch, H−1H-1, which we denote as V2V_{2}. To see this, observe that |V2||V_{2}| is at least ν​|JH−1|\nu|J_{H-1}| and they all arrive no earlier than tH−1t_{H-1}. Furthermore, the cost of V1V_{1} until tH−1t_{H-1} is at most tH−1​(1+ν)​|JH−1|≤tH−1​(1+ν)​|V2|​(1ν)t_{H-1}(1+\nu)|J_{H-1}|\leq t_{H-1}(1+\nu)|V_{2}|(\frac{1}{\nu}). So, we will have a competitive ratio of 1ν​(1+ν)\frac{1}{\nu}(1+\nu) in this charging.

Before bounding the waiting time for jobs in the final two sub-epochs, we discuss a subtlety in the analysis. Suppose the majority of jobs in V2V_{2} arrive shortly after tH−1t_{H-1}. In this case, these arrivals might not have a sufficiently large "arrival time window" to offset the cost incurred by jobs in JH−1J_{H-1} up to tHt_{H}. (The cost of JHJ_{H} through tH+1t_{H+1} can be easily handled, similar to the case with no sub-epochs or only the 00th epoch). However, in sub-epoch H−1H-1, we simulated the PF schedule based on the jobs in JH−1J_{H-1} while ignoring V2V_{2}. If we had to preempt sub-epoch H−1H-1 after simulating very few jobs up to what PF would have done, our non-preemptive simulation of PF in that interval may not be faithful to the actual PF schedule, meaning that the simulation time was effectively "wasted."

The remaining goal is to upper bound the waiting cost WW of JH−1J_{H-1} accumulating during the interval [tH−1,tH)[t_{H-1},t_{H}) (including V2V_{2}, the waiting cost will be a factor of 1+ν1+\nu larger). To upper bound WW, we consider several cases; in some cases, we will charge WW to specific subsequent epochs.

  1. 1.

    The last sub-epoch HH of epoch kk completes at least (ν/4)​|JH|(\nu/4)|J_{H}| jobs. We charge WW to the total completion time of these jobs, which increases the competitive ratio by a factor of Θ⁡(1/ν)\Theta(1/\nu). This charging is done “locally” within the same epoch, ensuring no overcharging.

  2. 2.

    Otherwise, let k′>kk^{\prime}>k be the latest epoch such that at least (ν/4)​|JH|(\nu/4)|J_{H}| jobs are completed during epochs k+1,k+2,…,k′k+1,k+2,\ldots,k^{\prime}.

    1. (a)

      If any of the epochs k+1,k+2,…,k′−1k+1,k+2,\ldots,k^{\prime}-1 has a sub-epoch—say k′′k^{\prime\prime} is the earliest epoch having a sub-epoch—then there must exist at least ν⁡(1−ν/2)​|JH|\nu(1-\nu/2)|J_{H}| jobs that arrive during epoch k′′k^{\prime\prime}. Each of these jobs has an arrival time greater than the waiting time of each job accounting for WW during sub-epoch H−1H-1 of epoch kk. Thus, we can charge WW to the total arrival time of these jobs, which increases the competitive ratio by at most O⁡(1/ν)O(1/\nu) additively. Note that this cross-epoch charging occurs to them only once, ensuring no overcharging.

    2. (b)

      Otherwise, we charge WW to the total completion time of jobs completed during epochs k+1,…,k′k+1,\ldots,k^{\prime}. Note that the waiting cost WW occurs during epoch kk (which has a sub-epoch) and it is charged to some of consecutive subsequent epochs that have no sub-epochs. Therefore, overcharging does not occur.

This completes the sketch of the analysis.

D.3 When predictions include overestimation

In this section, we show how to extend our results to cases where predictions include overestimation, i.e., p^j>pj\hat{p}_{j}>p_{j} for some jobs jj. We consider two strategies to handle this.

D.3.1 Strictly enforcing underestimation

The first approach is to ensure that no overestimation is effectively perceived by the algorithm. Specifically, if a job completes after receiving less than p^j\hat{p}_{j} units of processing, we treat the job as remaining active until it has received exactly p^j\hat{p}_{j} units. This is equivalent to processing jobs where each job jj has an effective size of max⁡{pj,p^j}\max\{p_{j},\hat{p}_{j}\} and a predicted size of p^j\hat{p}_{j}. Under this strategy, the bound in Theorem 3.3 becomes:

O⁡(1β​δ​∑jlog⁡(max⁡{pj,p^j}p^j+1))=O⁡(1β​δ​∑jlog⁡(pjp^j+1)).O\bigg(\frac{1}{\beta\delta}\sum_{j}\log\bigg(\frac{\max\{p_{j},\hat{p}_{j}\}}{\hat{p}_{j}}+1\bigg)\bigg)=O\bigg(\frac{1}{\beta\delta}\sum_{j}\log\bigg(\frac{p_{j}}{\hat{p}_{j}}+1\bigg)\bigg).

Thus, the asymptotic bound for preemptions remains unchanged. For the total completion time objective, this modification increases each job’s effective size by a factor of at most u:=maxj⁡p^j/pju:=\max_{j}\hat{p}_{j}/p_{j}. Since increasing every job size by a factor of uu increases the optimal objective by at most the same factor, the competitive ratio becomes 14.48​(1+ε)​u14.48(1+\varepsilon)u.

D.3.2 Weakly enforcing underestimation

Since overprediction has a significantly negative effect on the competitive ratio, we can intentionally underpredict job sizes at the cost of additional preemptions. If the number of overpredicted jobs is small and we have an upper bound gg on this quantity with high probability (w.h.p.), we can handle these cases more effectively. Intuitively, predicting a single global parameter—the total number of overpredicted jobs—is easier than identifying specifically which jobs are overpredicted.

Suppose we know that there are at most gg jobs with overpredicted sizes. We run the SNAP algorithm as before until the number of alive jobs drops to g/εg/\varepsilon or less. More specifically, at time eke_{k}, if nk≤g/εn_{k}\leq g/\varepsilon, we reset the predicted size of every alive job to the smallest power of 1+δ1+\delta that is no smaller than its current cumulative processed size. This effectively means that from this point forward, we ignore the original predictions to ensure we only deal with underpredictions. Let this transition occur at the beginning of epoch K′+1K^{\prime}+1. Another small caveat in running SNAP until epoch K′K^{\prime} is if a job turns out to be overestimated. So, a job may complete before it receives vj,kv_{j,k} units of processing in epoch kk but this can only reduce the current epoch’s length, which is only good for the algorithm.

Competitive ratio analysis.

The analysis then proceeds similarly. The primary difference is that until epoch K′K^{\prime}, we focus only on the underestimated jobs. That is, nkun^{u}_{k} denotes the number of underestimated jobs alive at eke_{k}. Lemma 3.5 is modified as follows:

Lemma D.1 (Modification of Lemma 3.5).

𝖺𝗅𝗀≤∑k=1K′(nku+g)​4​lk+∑k=K′+1Knku​4​lk≤4​(1+ε)​∑k=1Knku​lk.\mathsf{alg}\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K^{\prime}}(n^{u}_{k}+g)4l_{k}+\sum_{k=K^{\prime}+1}^{K}n^{u}_{k}4l_{k}\leq 4(1+\varepsilon)\sum_{k=1}^{K}n^{u}_{k}l_{k}.

Here, note that since epoch K′+1K^{\prime}+1, all jobs are effectively underestimated (in the analysis of the completion time objective only), thus, nk=nkun_{k}=n^{u}_{k} for all k≥K′+1k\geq K^{\prime}+1.

The subsequent claims, lemmas, and corollaries need only very minor changes. Let JkuJ^{u}_{k} be the subset of jobs in JkJ_{k} that are underestimated. We analogously restrict XkX_{k} and YkY_{k} to XkuX^{u}_{k} and YkuY^{u}_{k}, respectively.

Claim D.2 (Modification of Claim 3.6).

For each epoch kk, we have nku​lk≤2⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Jku)n^{u}_{k}l_{k}\leq 2\cdot\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in J^{u}_{k}).

For each epoch kk and any η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), we have,

𝗈𝗉𝗍⁡(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Jku)≤1η​𝗈𝗉𝗍​(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Xku)+11−η​𝗈𝗉𝗍​(lk​yj(k)∣j∈Yku).\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in J^{u}_{k})\leq\frac{1}{\eta}\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in X^{u}_{k})+\frac{1}{1-\eta}\mathsf{opt}(l_{k}y_{j}^{(k)}\mid j\in Y^{u}_{k})\ . (3)

We now turn our attention to upper-bounding the number of preemptions. By following exactly the same steps as the proof of Theorem 3.3, we can bound the number of preemptions until epoch K′K^{\prime} by:

Since we reset the predicted sizes of all jobs in JK′+1J_{K^{\prime}+1} such that they are all henceforth underestimated, we can apply Theorem 3.3. Letting pmax:=maxj⁡pjp_{\max}:=\max_{j}p_{j}, the number of preemptions for these jobs is at most:

Theorem D.7.

For any sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0, assuming there are at most gg overpredicted jobs, there exists an algorithm that is 14.48​(1+ε)14.48(1+\varepsilon)-competitive for minimizing total completion time while performing at most O⁡(1ε3​(∑jlog⁡(pjp^j+1)+gε​log⁡pmax))O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}(\sum_{j}\log(\frac{p_{j}}{\hat{p}_{j}}+1)+\frac{g}{\varepsilon}\log p_{\max})) preemptions and migrations.

Appendix E A general framework for PSP

In this section, we present the full description of our framework for PSP, and the proof of Theorem 4.4.

Our framework works in epochs 1,2,…,K1,2,\ldots,K. Epoch kk starts at time eke_{k} and ends at time ek+1e_{k+1}; Epoch 11 starts at time e1=0e_{1}=0. Let JkJ_{k} denote the set of available jobs at the start of epoch kk and let |Jk|=nk|J_{k}|=n_{k}. At time eke_{k}, we plan a complete schedule for epoch kk as described in the following:

  1. 1.

    Compute PF Rates. We compute the PF rates y(k)y^{(k)} for the jobs JkJ_{k}. Formally, y(k)y^{(k)} is the solution to

    (𝖢𝖯⁡(J))max∑j∈Jwj⋅log⁡(yj)s.t.∑j∈Jbd​j⋅yj≤1∀d∈[D]yj≥0∀j∈J\begin{array}[]{rr>{\displaystyle}rcl>{\quad}l}(\mathsf{CP}(J))&\operatorname{max}&\lx@intercol\displaystyle\sum_{j\in J}w_{j}\cdot\log(y_{j})\hfil\lx@intercol\\ &\text{s.t.}&\sum_{j\in J}b_{dj}\cdot y_{j}&\leq&1&\forall d\in[D]\\ &&y_{j}&\geq&0&\forall j\in J\end{array}
  2. 2.

    Compute Next Checkpoints. For each job j∈Jkj\in J_{k}, we define the remaining processing requirement to reach its next checkpoint as uj,k=(1+δ)h+1−qj​(ek)u_{j,k}=(1+\delta)^{h+1}-q_{j}(e_{k}), where h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N} s.t. (1+δ)h≤max⁡{qj​(ek),p^j}<(1+δ)h+1(1+\delta)^{h}\leq\max\{q_{j}(e_{k}),\hat{p}_{j}\}<(1+\delta)^{h+1}.

  3. 3.

    Determine the Simulation Duration. Let lkl_{k} denote the length of the shortest time interval such that, if jobs are processed at rates y(k)y^{(k)} during the time interval, at least ⌈β​nk⌉\lceil\beta n_{k}\rceil jobs from JkJ_{k} reach their next checkpoint. The targeted processing requirement for each job j∈Jkj\in J_{k} is then vj,k=min⁡{uj,k,lk​yj(k)}v_{j,k}=\min\{u_{j,k},l_{k}y^{(k)}_{j}\}.

  4. 4.

    Convert to a O⁡(1)O(1)-Preemptive Schedule. We now compute an α\alpha-approximate O⁡(1)O(1)-preemptive schedule (cf. Definition 4.1) for jobs JkJ_{k} with processing requirements vj,kv_{j,k} for each j∈Jkj\in J_{k}. If we start this schedule at time eke_{k}, it will complete by time at most ek+1≤ek+α​lke_{k+1}\leq e_{k}+\alpha l_{k}. Then, Epoch kk ends and we start Epoch k+1k+1 if not all jobs have been completed yet.

Theorem E.1.

The total number of preemptions performed by our framework is at most O⁡(1β​δ​∑j(1+log2⁡pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\beta\delta}\sum_{j}(1+\log_{2}p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})).

Proof.

In each epoch kk, the α\alpha-approximate O⁡(1)O(1)-preemptive schedule uses by definition at most O⁡(1)O(1) preemptions per job, so O⁡(nk)O(n_{k}) preemptions in total. By our choice of lkl_{k}, at least β​nk\beta n_{k} jobs each reach a checkpoint during epoch kk. Since there can be at most ∑j(1+⌈log1+δ⁡pj/p^j⌉)\sum_{j}(1+\lceil\log_{1+\delta}p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j}\rceil) checkpoints in total, there can be at most β⋅∑j(1+⌈log1+δ⁡pj/p^j⌉)\beta\cdot\sum_{j}(1+\lceil\log_{1+\delta}p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j}\rceil) many epochs. Thus, the total number of preemptions used by our algorithm is at most O⁡(1β​∑jlog1+δ⁡pj/p^j)=O⁡(1β​δ​∑j(1+log2⁡pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{j}\log_{1+\delta}p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})=O(\frac{1}{\beta\delta}\sum_{j}(1+\log_{2}p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})). ∎

Lemma E.2.

For any β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), the virtual algorithm achieves a total weighted completion time at most 27​(1+δ)(1−β)3\frac{27(1+\delta)}{(1-\beta)^{3}} times the optimum for PSP.

Proof.

Consider any epoch kk in the schedule SS of the virtual algorithm for this epoch. For simplicity, we assume without loss of generality that epoch kk starts at time 00 and ends at time lkl_{k}. Let XkX_{k} denote the set of jobs that reach their next checkpoint during epoch kk. For each XkX_{k}, let lj,kl_{j,k} denote the time at which job jj reaches its next checkpoint, that is, a processing requirement of vj,kv_{j,k}.

We next construct an instance Ik′I^{\prime}_{k} for β\beta-robust PSP. PF’s initial rates yy for Ik′I^{\prime}_{k} are equal to y(k)y^{(k)}, as both are based on the set of jobs JkJ_{k} and the rates are unique. For any time t∈[0,lk]t\in[0,l_{k}], we choose the nullified set of jobs to be N⁡(t)={j∈Xk∣t≤lk−lj,k}N(t)=\{j\in X_{k}\mid t\leq l_{k}-l_{j,k}\}. For each job j∈Xkj\in X_{k}, we have that j∈N⁡(t)j\in N(t) for all t∈[0,lj,k]t\in[0,l_{j,k}]. In conclusion, the total weighted completion time of PF for Ik′I^{\prime}_{k}, denoted by PF⁡(Ik′)\mathrm{PF}(I^{\prime}_{k}), is at most nk​lkn_{k}l_{k}.

Similarly to Lemma 3.5, we have

𝖺𝗅𝗀v​i​r​t≤∑k≥1nk​lk=∑k≥1PF⁡(Ik′).\mathsf{alg}^{virt}\leq\sum_{k\geq 1}n_{k}l_{k}=\sum_{k\geq 1}\mathrm{PF}(I^{\prime}_{k})\ .

Now we can concatenate all instances Ik′I^{\prime}_{k} to form a new instance I′I^{\prime}. It is easy to check that this is again a β\beta-robust PSP instance where each job jj has a total processing requirement equal to pjp_{j}. Moreover, the total weighted completion time of PF for I′I^{\prime} is equal to ∑k≥0PF⁡(Ik′)\sum_{k\geq 0}\mathrm{PF}(I^{\prime}_{k}). Therefore,

Since the total completion time of the framework is at most α\alpha times the total completion time of the virtual algorithm, Theorem E.1 and Lemma E.2 imply Theorem 4.4.

Appendix F Application to malleable scheduling

We apply our framework to malleable job scheduling on identical and unrelated machines. We are given a set of machines MM and for every job j∈Jj\in J a speed-up function fj:ℝ≥0→ℝ≥0f_{j}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}. In a job-to-machine assignment, let xi​j​(t)x_{ij}(t) be the fraction of machine ii given to job jj at time tt. The processing rate of job jj at time tt is given by fj​(∑isi​j​xi​j​(t))f_{j}(\sum_{i}s_{ij}x_{ij}(t)). We assume that each fjf_{j} is non-decreasing and concave. This is a PSP with the rate polytope 𝒫={f(x)∣∑i∈Mxi​j≤1∀j∈J,∑j∈Jxi​j≤1∀i∈M}\mathcal{P}=\{f(x)\mid\sum_{i\in M}x_{ij}\leq 1\,\forall j\in J,\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}\leq 1\forall i\in M\}; see [IKM18] for details.

We present algorithms for computing α\alpha-approximate O⁡(1)O(1)-preemptive schedules (cf. Definition 4.1), which together with Theorem 4.4 imply competitive algorithms with few preemptions.

We start with the case of mm identical parallel machines. Here, we additionally assume that each function fjf_{j} is piecewise linear with breakpoints at integers points.

Theorem F.1.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is a 54​(1+ε)54(1+\varepsilon)-competitive algorithm that incurs at most O⁡(1ε2​∑j(1+log2⁡pj/p^j))O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}\sum_{j}(1+\log_{2}p_{j}/\hat{p}_{j})) preemptions for minimizing the total completion time for malleable job scheduling on identical parallel machines if each function fjf_{j} is piecewise linear with breakpoints at integer points.

Proof.

We provide an algorithm for computing 22-approximate 00-preemptive schedules for the problem. The theorem then follows from Theorem 4.4.

Consider fixed rates yy that correspond to a fractional schedule. where each job jj is assigned to xjx_{j} machines and a length LL. Let J1={j∣xj≥1}J_{1}=\{j\mid x_{j}\geq 1\} and J2={j∣xj<1}J_{2}=\{j\mid x_{j}<1\}. We create a non-preemptive integral schedule as follows: For each job j∈J1j\in J_{1}, we assign job jj to ⌊xj⌋\lfloor x_{j}\rfloor machines MjM_{j} and those machines only work on job jj throughout the whole schedule. Since fjf_{j} is concave and piecewise linear with breakpoints at integers, and since xj≥1x_{j}\geq 1, we have fj​(xj)≤2​fj​(⌊xj⌋)f_{j}(x_{j})\leq 2f_{j}(\lfloor x_{j}\rfloor). Thus, the completion time of jj in the integral schedule is at most 2​L2L. Note that jobs in J1J_{1} use at most m1=⌊∑j∈J1xj⌋m_{1}=\lfloor\sum_{j\in J_{1}}x_{j}\rfloor many machines. Next, consider all jobs j∈J2j\in J_{2}. We greedily schedule those jobs on the remaining m−m1=⌈∑j∈J2xj⌉m-m_{1}=\lceil\sum_{j\in J_{2}}x_{j}\rceil machines via list scheduling, where each job gets one machine until it finishes. By the well-known list scheduling properties, this ensures that all jobs in J2J_{2} complete within at most 2​L2L time. Since no job is preempted, this completes the proof of the theorem. ∎

We next present our results for unrelated machines. For this problem we additionally assume that fj​(s)⋅sf_{j}(s)\cdot s is non-increasing as a function of ss. This is a common non-decreasing work assumption, see e.g., [FMP23].
