Appendix G Proportional Fairness for β\beta-robust PSP

In this section, we analyze PF for β\beta-robust PSP and show Theorem 4.3, which we first restate. Our analysis holds even for the setting where jobs arrive online over time at their release dates rjr_{j}.

See 4.3

We first restate the PF algorithm. At every time tt, it computes the processing allocation y⁡(t)y(t) that is optimal for the following convex program 𝖢𝖯⁡(J⁡(t))\mathsf{CP}(J(t)) for the active jobs J⁡(t)J(t) at time tt.

(𝖢𝖯⁡(J))max∑j∈Jwj⋅log⁡(yj)s.t.∑j∈Jbd​j⋅yj≤1∀d∈[D]yj≥0∀j∈J\begin{array}[]{rr>{\displaystyle}rcl>{\quad}l}(\mathsf{CP}(J))&\operatorname{max}&\lx@intercol\displaystyle\sum_{j\in J}w_{j}\cdot\log(y_{j})\hfil\lx@intercol\\ &\text{s.t.}&\sum_{j\in J}b_{dj}\cdot y_{j}&\leq&1&\forall d\in[D]\\ &&y_{j}&\geq&0&\forall j\in J\end{array}

In the β\beta-robust PSP setting, the adversary can then select a set of jobs N⁡(t)⊆J⁡(t)N(t)\subseteq J(t) such that |N⁡(t)|≤β⋅|J⁡(t)||N(t)|\leq\beta\cdot|J(t)|, for some fixed β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1). The final processing allocation of the algorithm is then

y^j​(t):={0if ​j∈N⁡(t)yj​(t)else.\hat{y}_{j}(t):=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }j\in N(t)\\ y_{j}(t)&\text{else.}\end{cases}

Note that if y⁡(t)∈𝒫y(t)\in{\mathcal{P}} then also y^​(t)∈𝒫\hat{y}(t)\in{\mathcal{P}} since we assume that 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} is downward closed.

Our analysis is based on the analysis of PF for PSP [IKM18, JLM26]. Our main contribution here is to carefully integrate that changed rates of nullified jobs into the traditional analysis. A critical issue is that the new rate vector y^\hat{y} is not necessarily an optimal solution to 𝖢𝖯⁡(J)\mathsf{CP}(J) and thus does not satisfy crucial optimality conditions on which the proof in [IKM18, JLM26] relies on.

G.1 KKT conditions

To characterize the optimal solution of (𝖢𝖯⁡(J))(\mathsf{CP}(J)), we consider its KKT conditions for the Lagrange multipliers ηd\eta_{d} for each d∈[D]d\in[D] [BV04].

1yj−∑d=1Dbd​j​ηd\displaystyle\frac{1}{y_{j}}-\sum_{d=1}^{D}b_{dj}\eta_{d} =0∀j∈J\displaystyle=0\quad\forall j\in J (6)
ηd⋅(1−∑j∈Jbd​j​yj)\displaystyle\eta_{d}\cdot\biggl(1-\sum_{j\in J}b_{dj}y_{j}\biggr) =0∀d∈[D]\displaystyle=0\quad\forall d\in[D] (7)
ηd\displaystyle\eta_{d} ≥0∀d∈[D]\displaystyle\geq 0\quad\forall d\in[D] (8)

A direct consequence of the KKT conditions is the following lemma, which is a classic connection between the number of active jobs and their dual multipliers [IKM18, EG59]. We refer to [IKM18, JLM26] for a proof.

Lemma G.1 ([IKM18]).

Let JJ be a set of jobs, and let η\eta be optimal Lagrange multipliers for (𝖢𝖯⁡(J))(\mathsf{CP}(J)). Then ∑d=1Dηd=|J|\sum_{d=1}^{D}\eta_{d}=|J|.

G.2 Linear programming relaxation

We compare the performance of PF to an optimal schedule that is allowed to run at a slower speed. More precisely, we compare PF to an optimal solution that runs at speed 1/κ1/\kappa for some parameter κ≥1\kappa\geq 1. The following linear program is a relaxation of this optimal solution, where the variables yj​ty_{jt} indicate the total amount of processing that job jj receives in the interval [t,t+1][t,t+1].

Appendix H Other related work

Since various objectives are considered in the literature, we mostly focus on the total (weighted) completion time objective. Unless otherwise specified, we assume that preemption is permitted in the results discussed below. For brevity, “completion time” will hereafter refer to the objective of minimizing the sum of completion times.

Single Machine: In the clairvoyant scenario, it is folklore that Shortest Remaining Time First (SRPT) is optimal. Note that SRPT becomes Shortest Job First (SJF), which processes jobs in non-decreasing order of their processing time. For non-clairvoyant scheduling, Round-robin (RR) is known to be 22-competitive for completion time, which is the best competitive ratio achievable in this setting [MPT94]. Shortest Elapsed Time First (SETF) processes all jobs that have received the least amount of processing equally; note that SETF coincides with RR if all jobs arrive simultaneously. Recently, it was shown that SETF is 22-competitive for (weighted) completion time [Jäg+23].

While being O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive, both SETF and RR incur excessively many preemptions. Multilevel (Adaptive) Feedback (MLF) seeks to minimize the number of preemptions while retaining O⁡(1)O(1)-competitiveness for completion time. MLF can be parameterized to achieve a (2+ϵ)(2+\epsilon)-competitive ratio for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 [MPT94].

Identical Machines: The performance guarantees of SRPT and RR for a single machine extend to parallel identical machines [MPT94, Bea+12]; see also [Den+00, MV22a] for closely related work. Under the resource augmentation framework, SETF is shown to be O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive for identical machines [KP00].

Completion Time vs. Flow Time: The optimal schedule for total completion time is identical to that of the total flow time objective, where a job’s flow time is defined as Fj=Cj−rjF_{j}=C_{j}-r_{j}. However, from an approximation and competitive analysis standpoint, the flow time objective is significantly more challenging. Consequently, online algorithms are often provided with extra speed and compared against the offline optimum. It is well-established that an algorithm that is O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive with O⁡(1)O(1)-speed for flow time is also O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive for completion time. For example, while [KP00] primarily studies flow time minimization, their results readily translate to the completion time objective.

Unrelated Machines: In the offline setting, minimizing total completion time on unrelated machines is solvable in polynomial time if all jobs arrive at t=0t=0. If jobs have release times, the problem becomes NP-hard and, in fact, APX-hard [HSW98]. Constant-factor approximations are well-established [SS02, Sku01, SS99, BSS16, IL23, Har24], and the current state-of-the-art approximation ratio is 1.36+ε1.36+\varepsilon due to [Li25]. In the clairvoyant online setting, utilizing immediate-dispatch and non-migratory algorithms while assuming each machine runs SPT or SRPT, assigning an arriving job to the machine with the least marginal increase in the objective is O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive [AGK12, Gup+20]. For non-clairvoyant algorithms, SelfishMigrate and Proportional Fairness (PF) were analyzed with competitive ratios of 3232 and 4.624.62, respectively [Im+14, JLM26]. Various clairvoyant algorithms were also explored in [Hal+97, Cha+96, LMR23].

Polytope Scheduling: Polytope scheduling is a general framework that captures various scheduling objectives and encompasses all the aforementioned problems. For this general scheduling problem, [IKM18] showed that Proportional Fairness (PF) is 128128-competitive for total weighted completion time, a result that was later improved to 2727 by [JLM26]. Furthermore, [JLM26] demonstrated that PF achieves surprisingly strong competitive ratios for various special cases, including the unrelated machines setting.

Online Scheduling with Predictions: As alluded to previously, scheduling has become a primary application for ML-augmented algorithms. Various objectives were considered. For example, total completion time [PSK18, Im+23, LM25, Din+22], total flow time [ALT21, Mit20], makespan minimization [Lat+20, LX21, Bal+25], and minimizing energy consumption [Bam+20, AJS22].

Appendix I Further experimental details and results

I.1 Algorithm details

We provide further details of the algorithms.

  1. 1.

    SNAP (coupled with PMLF): Recall that the SNAP algorithm aims to process each job jj by vj,kv_{j,k} units in epoch kk. While a machine ii could technically idle after meeting the specific processing targets vj,kv_{j,k} for its assigned jobs, such idling results in an unnecessary loss of efficiency.

    Therefore, we introduce an engineering adaptation: while jobs are assigned to machines following Step 4, we execute the PMLF (Preemptive Multi-Level Feedback) policy on each individual machine to process its assigned jobs. An epoch concludes once a β\beta fraction of jobs are exhausted.

    This approach serves as a practical adaptation that maintains the underlying spirit and analysis of SNAP. Each epoch is designed to exhaust a constant fraction of jobs, mimicking the schedule of PF (Proportional Fairness). This behavior is indirectly achieved through PMLF; we know Step 4 processes jobs without exhausting more than β​nk\beta n_{k} jobs within 4​lk4l_{k} time steps. Given vj,k=lk​yj(k)v_{j,k}=l_{k}y^{(k)}_{j} for each job j∈Fkj\in F_{k} where |Fk|=(1−β)​nk|F_{k}|=(1-\beta)n_{k}, exhausting more than β​nk\beta n_{k} jobs ensures we are effectively mimicking PF without being constrained by rigid checkpoints. This provides the intuition for using PMLF.

  2. 2.

    Blind Algorithm: This policy is non-migratory, ensuring that no job is ever processed on multiple machines throughout its duration. The algorithm is equivalent to that of [AGK12] assuming that pj=p^jp_{j}=\hat{p}_{j} for all jobs jj. The algorithm operates under the assumption of 100%100\% trust in the provided predictions. Let tt denote the current time and qj​(t)q_{j}(t) represent the volume of job jj processed prior to tt. The predicted remaining size of job jj is thus given by p^j−qj​(t)\hat{p}_{j}-q_{j}(t).

    On each machine ii, we execute the Shortest Job First (SJF) policy (or equivalently SRPT). We define the residual estimate for machine ii as the total completion time that would be incurred by running SJF on that machine based on these predicted remaining sizes.

    Upon the arrival of a new job with a predicted size, we compute the potential increase in the residual estimate for every machine. The job is then assigned to the machine that yields the minimum marginal increase to the total residual estimate.

  3. 3.

    Doubling (Coupled With Immediate-Dispatch): Initially, each job’s size is assumed to be equal to its predicted size p^j\hat{p}_{j}. If a job’s actual processing time exceeds this estimate, we double the predicted size (i.e., p^j←2​p^j\hat{p}_{j}\leftarrow 2\hat{p}_{j}). In this event, we treat the original job as completed and consider a new copy of the job to have arrived. This copy is dispatched to the machine that results in the minimum increase to the residual estimate.

  4. 4.

    Hybrid SNAP: Initially, all jobs are initially in Group 1. Jobs in Group 1 are dispatched to machines using the Doubling strategy. To loosely emulate the Blind strategy, we utilize large milestones: {c​(1+δ)i​p^j∣i≥1}\{c(1+\delta)^{i}\hat{p}_{j}\mid i\geq 1\} for a large parameter c≥1c\geq 1. Any job that reaches its first milestone permanently migrates to Group 2. Group 2 jobs are assigned to machines using the SNAP algorithm. Finally, we execute PMLF on individual machines to process their assigned jobs.

I.2 Further experimental results

We conduct further experiments to evaluate the performance of our algorithms. The first experiment investigates the competitive ratio and preemption frequency of SNAP as a function of the exhaustion parameter β\beta, with δ=1\delta=1 and R=512R=512. Interestingly, SNAP exhibits a remarkably stable competitive ratio for most values of β\beta; the performance degrades sharply only when β\beta reaches 100%100\%. In contrast, the preemption frequency is highly sensitive to β\beta, decreasing significantly as β\beta increases. Note that since other algorithms do not utilize the β\beta parameter, their performance remains constant across these values.

The second experiment compares the algorithms across various values of δ\delta. In our implementation, δ\delta defines the checkpoints for SNAP and serves as a parameter for the PMLF subprocedure. Intuitively, a larger δ\delta implies a higher threshold for processing before a preemption occurs. Similarly, our implementation of SelfishMigrate utilizes δ\delta within its SNAP subprocedure. In the Doubling approach, we simulate a job completion and the release of a new job whenever the processing reaches a power of (1+δ)(1+\delta). Thus, while the algorithms (with the exception of Blind) utilize δ\delta differently, the parameter serves a similar purpose across all of them. For this experiment, we set β=0.6\beta=0.6 and R=512R=512. As δ\delta increases, the competitive ratios of Doubling and SelfishMigrate increase mildly, while that of SNAP decreases slightly. However, the impact of δ\delta on preemption frequency is more pronounced: the frequency drops consistently as δ\delta increases across all applicable algorithms.

Our final experiment evaluates Hybrid SNAP by comparing the competitive ratios of the algorithms across different special job and machine frequencies, with parameters set at β=0.7\beta=0.7 and R=256R=256. We observe that in the absence of special jobs, the Blind algorithm performs effectively. This is because the machines are essentially identical in this scenario, allowing even a blind strategy to achieve efficient load balancing across resources. However, once heterogeneity is introduced (across all tested frequencies from 10% to 50%), SNAP and Hybrid SNAP consistently yield the superior competitive ratios. In particular, Hybrid SNAP with c=8c=8 significantly outperforms both Blind and Doubling. This experiment demonstrates the robust performance of our proposed algorithms across varying degrees of system heterogeneity.

Appendix J Reproducibility and code implementation

Initial implementations of the experimental code and plotting scripts were generated using Gemini 3 Pro. All generated code was subsequently refactored, manually verified, and rigorously tested to ensure the technical accuracy of the algorithm’s implementation and the reproducibility of the results. The full source code is provided in the supplemental material.
